docs.summary: Add components to an integration, document their public contract, and make them work in every app that installs the package.

blocks.text: In global mode: components from an integration installed for the computer show up outside projects; inside a project, only components from integrations the project installs. See {@link namespace:global} and {@link generic:global-integrations}.

docs.name: computer-agent-guide
docs.title: The agent guide on your computer
docs.description: Your global install keeps one short Astryx skill in your home folder and links it into the folders agent tools read, so agents anywhere know Astryx is there. `{@command init --user}` writes it now or turns it off.

content.text: A project's agent docs reach only agents working in that project. Your global install also keeps one skill file, `~/.agents/skills/astryx/SKILL.md`, which most coding agents read. It tells agents that Astryx is on this computer, when it is relevant (building or changing UI), and to start with `{@command search}`. It names no version, so it never goes stale. Inside a project, the project's own agent docs come first.
It is written in the background on the first run and again after you upgrade, so no command waits for it. Installing the package does not write it, because some package managers skip install scripts.

Agents that read only their own skills folder get a link to the skill's folder, so they read the same one file: a folder symlink with a relative target (a junction on Windows, or a copy where neither can be made). Continue's scanner skips links, so it gets a copy, refreshed with the file:

rows: When Xcode's coding assistant folder exists

content.text: Astryx never replaces anything it did not create at one of these folders, and never writes a folder another tool manages; `{@command doctor}` names any it skipped, and any link whose skill folder is missing, as in a container that mounts only one agent's folder.

items: Cloud and background agents read only the repository, so the project's own agent docs, the block `{@command init}` writes into AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md, are what reach them.
Apps that take an uploaded skill: upload `~/.agents/skills/astryx/SKILL.md`, or a zip of its folder.

content.text: If your agent reads skills from another folder, link it to the skill:

content.code: ln -s ~/.agents/skills/astryx <your agent's skills folder>/astryx

content.text: On Windows, in PowerShell:

content.code: New-Item -ItemType Junction -Path "<your agent's skills folder>\astryx" -Target "$HOME\.agents\skills\astryx"

sections.title: Write it now, or turn it off

content.code:
{@command init --user}
{@command init --user --remove-agents}

items: `init --user` writes the file and the links now.
`--remove-agents` removes the file and every link Astryx made, and turns it off until you run `{@command init --user}` again.
A file you edited is never overwritten or removed; delete it to get the current text.
Outside a project, `{@command doctor}` says whether the skill is there, current, edited, or turned off, and where it is linked.

content.text: This page is part of {@link namespace:global}, which explains what global mode is and how each part works. A project's own agent docs: {@link command:init}.

docs.name: computer-integrations
docs.title: Integrations installed globally
docs.description: Integrations installed next to your global install work in folders outside any project. Inside a project, only the integrations the project installs work, and the others are listed as ones you could add.

content.text: Install the integration the same way you installed the CLI, so the two sit side by side:

content.code: {@pm install @astryxdesign/cli @acme/widgets --global}

content.text: A tool that installs the CLI together with integrations in one folder, and runs the CLI from there, counts the same way. `npx` and the cache of project versions never count.

In a folder outside any project, Astryx loads each integration installed next to your global install the way a project loads its own: its components, templates, docs, themes, and discover source show up, and a command name it declares starts the commands Astryx prints. One whose `@astryxdesign/core` or `@astryxdesign/cli` peer range leaves out your global version is skipped, and `{@command doctor}` says why.

sections.title: Inside a project, only the project's

content.text: A project's answers must match what it installs: a component from a package it does not install would not build. So inside a project, an integration installed only globally adds nothing. `{@command discover}` lists it among the packages the project could add, with the project's install command, when it supports the project's version and loads. When the project installs the same integration, the project's copy is the one used.

items: Outside a project, `{@command doctor}` lists the global integrations it uses and warns about each it skips.
Inside a project, `{@command doctor}` and `{@command discover}` list the ones the project could add.

content.text: This page is part of {@link namespace:global}, which explains what global mode is and how each part works. Building an integration: {@link generic:global-integrations}.

docs.name: configuration
docs.title: Configuration
docs.summary: Set how your integration behaves in an app: agent guidance, the command your users run, debug and gap reports, and more as it grows.

blocks.text: In global mode: installed for the computer, beside the global CLI, your package's manifest is read as it is in a project and applies in folders outside any project; peer ranges are checked against the global CLI's release. See {@link namespace:global} and {@link generic:global-integrations}.

Beyond the things you ship, an integration can set how it behaves in an app: the guidance it gives the AI agents working there, the command its users run the CLI with, and the record it keeps of each CLI run. Open one below to set it up.

docs.name: css-and-stylex
docs.title: CSS & StyleX
docs.description: Core integration principle, plain CSS / CSS Modules, and StyleX typed-token imports.

content.text: Keep the system as the source of truth for theme values. Components read design tokens from CSS custom properties such as `--color-text-primary`, `--color-background-surface`, `--spacing-4`, and `--radius-container`. Other styling libraries should map their own semantic tokens, utility names, or theme objects to those system CSS variables whenever possible.

Use CSS variables for ordinary DOM styling because they inherit through the tree, follow `data-theme` color mode, respect nested `data-astryx-theme` scopes, and update when themes switch. Use token resolver APIs only for non-CSS consumers such as SVG attribute values, canvas, chart configuration, color calculations, or static config generation.

For available token names and values, run {@link namespace:tokens}. Focused references are also available with {@link generic:color}, {@link generic:spacing}, {@link generic:shape}, {@link namespace:typography}, {@link generic:elevation}, and {@link generic:motion}.

Choose the narrowest integration path that fits the styling library. Most DOM styling should stay on the CSS-variable path; JavaScript token resolution is for APIs that cannot consume CSS custom properties.

rows: The library ultimately writes CSS and accepts string values
You are writing StyleX styles in application code
You want utility classes backed by active system tokens
JavaScript needs token values for charts, canvas, SVG, or config objects

items: Map by semantic intent: text, surface, border, accent, status, radius, spacing, typography.
Let the system own color mode. The root Theme syncs `data-theme="light|dark"` and `data-astryx-theme` to `<html>` for portals and first-level theme scope.
Prefer CSS variables for runtime theme switching and nested themes.
Copy raw hex/px values into a second theme object when a `var(...)` reference would work.
Run a second unsynchronized dark-mode provider that disagrees with Theme.
Make another library's CSS variables the source of truth for the system. Some consumers need token values outside the DOM.

content.text: The simplest integration is direct CSS variable usage. CSS Modules scope class names, but system token variables are global/inherited values supplied by package CSS and the active theme.

content.label: Card.module.css

content.text: Sass variables are compile-time only. They are useful for generating static CSS, but they do not update when the system switches theme or color mode. Use native CSS custom properties for themeable values.

For StyleX styles, prefer the typed token exports from `@astryxdesign/core/theme/tokens.stylex`. They provide autocomplete and catch token-name typos while still resolving through the same system CSS variables at runtime.

content.label: Typed token imports

content.text: Use `xstyle` for component overrides and `stylex.props()` for your own DOM nodes. Use `className` when integrating a non-StyleX styling library.

docs.name: debug-and-gap-reports
docs.title: Debug and gap reports
docs.description: Receive a record of each CLI run in apps that use your package, and handle the gap reports they send about it.

content.text: Export a `debug` function from `astryx.integration.mjs`; the CLI calls it once per command run in an app loading your package.
The event is a `DebugEvent` with `command`, `outcome`, `exitCode`, `durationMs`, `error`, and more, its values scrubbed (`redacted: true`). Every field is in {@link schema:debug-event}.

Keep the function synchronous: the CLI calls it as the process exits and never waits for a promise. The app's own `debug` handler runs first, then yours. A handler that throws is skipped, and the command's output and exit code stay the same.

An app records every command only when its `astryx.config` names `integrations` or `debug`, as listing your package does. Otherwise your handler runs only for commands loading the app's project, such as `component` and `docs`, never for `--version` or a mistyped command. In an app whose config names neither word, those commands also print a stderr warning.
`debug` is a named export, not a manifest field, so an older CLI ignores it and loads the rest of your manifest.

sections.title: Turn off debug in an app

content.text: An app can refuse every integration's `debug` handler and keep its own. It sets `inheritDebug` in its package.json:

content.code: {"astryx": {"inheritDebug": false}}

content.text: Your handler then no longer runs in that app.
Export a `gapReport` handler, and `{@command gap-report}` in an app sends it each gap report, such as a missing component or variant. The handler files the report and returns a receipt.
Every handler in the app gets every report, so check `report.target.package` and skip reports about other packages.
Every field is in {@link schema:gap-report-handler}.

The CLI waits 30 seconds, then aborts `signal`. A throw, a timeout, or an invalid receipt fails your delivery, and the command exits 1; the other handlers still run. Like `debug`, `gapReport` is a named export that older CLIs ignore.
Set `audience: 'public'` when your handler writes somewhere the public can read. The CLI runs it only when the caller passes `--confirm-public`; an `'internal'` handler always runs.

content.code: {@command gap-report AcmeCarousel --category missing_variant --reason 'Need a vertical layout'}

handlerType: integration
handler:     @acme/astryx-widgets
audience:    public
status:      consent_required
message:     Rerun with --confirm-public to file this report.

content.text: With `--confirm-public`, the same delivery reads `status: filed` and shows your `url`. The report goes to the package named by `--package`, else the package that owns the component, else Core.
With no `gapReport` handler in the app, the CLI routes the report to the target package's manifest `issuesUrl`.

items: A GitHub issues URL, such as `https://github.com/acme/widgets/issues`, gets an issue filed with the GitHub CLI, `gh`, once the caller passes `--confirm-public`.
Any other URL comes back as a `routed_only` receipt for the caller to open.
With no `issuesUrl`, the command fails: `Package "@acme/astryx-widgets" provides neither a report handler nor an issues URL.`

content.text: One handler anywhere in the app, from the app or from any package, turns the fallback off for every report. So does a listed package that fails to load: the CLI cannot tell whether it has a handler, so the report fails for that package instead of going to another tracker. See {@link command:gap-report}.

sections.title: Let the person choose where a report goes

content.text: When an app loads packages naming their own `issuesUrl`, a report can go to the default (the handlers, or the fallback above) or to one of those packages. `{@command gap-report --list-categories}` and the receipt of a report filed without `--to` list every destination, with a line telling the agent to ask the person.

items: An agent asks the person where to file. It never picks a package destination on its own.
`--to <package>` carries the person's choice: the report goes only to that package's `issuesUrl`, under the same `--confirm-public` rule, and no handler runs.
Without a choice, leave out `--to`; the report goes to the default.
A `--to` that names no destination fails before anything is sent and lists the destinations.

content.text: In global mode: when users install your package for their computer, beside the global CLI, its `debug` function receives runs in folders outside any project too; inside a project, only if the project installs it. See {@link namespace:global} and {@link generic:global-integrations}.

docs.name: define-the-theme
docs.title: Define the theme
docs.description: Point theme tokens at the palette, keep light-dark() to colors, and avoid Core internals.

content.text: A theme token is a named slot that Astryx components read for a value — `--color-accent` for the accent color, and so on. Components never read your palette directly; they read tokens. Defining a theme means pointing each token at a palette shade, so the components wear your colors.
Import the palette in `oceanTheme.ts` and point your tokens at its stops. Each token takes a `[light, dark]` pair — the shade to use in light mode and the one in dark mode.

Local imports must stay inside the theme folder. One that leaves it, such as `../../shared/colors`, fails with `invalid_theme`, and every theme in the package disappears from `theme list`. `{@command theme template}` writes a file that explains every `defineTheme` field. For the full token set and component theming, read {@link generic:author-a-theme}.

To base a theme on an existing one, `extends` it: import the base theme and override only the tokens you change. Add the derived theme with `integration add theme ocean-contrast`, and import the base from its built package export, since local imports cannot leave the theme folder. The derived theme keeps a live link to the base and picks up its later changes when you rebuild it — unlike `--from`, which forks a copy ({@link generic:add-a-theme}).

Each `[light, dark]` pair compiles to a `light-dark()` value, which switches only colors. Give it colors. For a value that is not a plain color — a gradient — put `light-dark()` on each color stop, not around the whole value: `light-dark()` takes two colors, so wrapping whole gradients makes the value invalid where the token is used, and `theme build` does not warn.

sections.title: Do not set Core private variables

content.text: Core private variables start with `--_`, such as `--_field-radius`. They are internals and can change in any Core release, so `theme build` reports each one it finds as an `[error]`. Set the standard CSS property instead — `borderRadius`, `padding` — and let the build emit the internal variable where Core needs it.

The theme imports `@astryxdesign/core/theme`, so declare Core as a peer dependency, with the range of Core versions you test the theme against — a range, not an exact version, so a Core patch release does not force a republish. `integration add theme` already declared the optional `@astryxdesign/cli` peer that reads themes:

docs.name: describe-the-component
docs.title: Describe the component
docs.summary: Write and maintain the default component doc, then adapt it when one family owns several exports or a member needs its own file.

blocks.text: A component's `.doc.mjs` is part of the integration's public contract, not optional commentary. Astryx uses it for CLI output and search, and people and agents read it to decide whether the component fits and how to use it.

items: Change the source and its `.doc.mjs` together.
Update the doc whenever the public name, import, behavior, props, defaults, examples, or accessibility requirements change.

`integration verify` checks the doc shape and packed import, and `doctor integration components` compares each props table with the component's TypeScript props ({@link generic:check-the-props}). Neither can prove the prose still matches the component.

blocks.text: Every component doc has one stable identity and enough usage guidance for a reader to choose it correctly. Pick the shape below that matches your module.
After every source or doc change, read the component back. This output is what people and agents receive.

docs.name: docs
docs.title: Docs
docs.summary: Write docs that ship with your package and that people and agents find by search or one level at a time.

blocks.text: In global mode: docs from an integration installed for the computer show up outside projects; inside a project, only docs from integrations the project installs. See {@link namespace:global} and {@link generic:global-integrations}.

docs.name: doc-syntax
docs.title: Doc syntax
docs.description: The tokens a doc writes for links, Astryx commands and package-manager steps, which the CLI shows each reader in their own package manager.

content.text: A doc never names a package manager or a runner: readers use npm, pnpm, Yarn or Bun, and run the CLI through their own. Write a token instead, and the CLI shows each reader the command they run. Tokens work in prose, list items, table cells and code blocks.

rows: the command that opens that doc
a step only one package manager can do
`npm pkg set name=x` (only with npm: why)

content.text: In prose a token prints as a code span; in a code span or code block it prints as the command alone. `--json` carries the same commands, a `{@@command}` token as the bare command that starts with astryx, which a reader that shows the doc prefixes itself.
A `{@@pm}` token is a verb, its names, and the flags it takes. Each row below runs the same way in every package manager; the CLI writes the reader's own.

rows: `yarn global add x` (Yarn 1); npm on Yarn 2 and newer

items: Flags: `--dev` and `--exact` with `install`, `--global` with `install` and `remove`, `--latest` with `update`. `--exact` takes one version, never a range: only npm pins a range.
Everything after the name of a script (`run`), a binary (`exec`) or a package (`dlx`, `create`) is passed to it as written.
`{@@pm install x --global}` on pnpm needs `pnpm setup` once per computer.

sections.title: A step only one package manager can do

content.text: Some commands exist in one package manager only, such as `npm pkg set` or `pnpm setup`. Write `{@@pm-only <manager> "<reason>" <command>}`: the manager is one of npm, pnpm, yarn, yarn-classic or bun, and the reason, in double quotes, is shown to readers beside the command. Use it only when no `{@@pm}` step does the same: doctor names a one-manager step that every package manager can run, with the `{@@pm}` token to write.

`doctor integration validate`, and so `integration check`, lists each of these as a note with its file, line and the token to write. A note fails nothing today; the next minor release turns them into warnings, so `integration check --strict --next` fails on them now. Run it to fix them ahead.

rows: a code span or shell line written for one package manager, such as `npm install -D x`
an Astryx command written with a runner, such as `pnpm exec astryx docs`
an Astryx command written bare, where `{@@command docs}` checks that the command exists
a token that does not parse, or a name that is not a doc token

content.text: In global mode: outside a project, a `{@@command}` token prints the way your global install prints every command, and a `{@@pm}` step prints for npm unless the CLI detects another package manager. In a project, the project's own runner and package manager decide. See {@link namespace:global}.

docs.name: document-the-template
docs.title: Document the template
docs.summary: Write the doc that helps people and agents find, choose, and trust your template: its name, description, readiness, preview, and any Core replacement.

docs.name: document-the-theme
docs.title: Document the theme
docs.description: Document a theme by extending the core theme topic, so an app reads it in {@link generic:theme}.

content.text: Give your theme a doc topic that extends the core `theme` topic, so an app that lists your package sees your theme at the end of {@link generic:theme}. Add it with `extends: 'theme'` ({@link generic:extend-or-replace}).

Keep the section short: how to install the package, run `theme add`, apply the generated module ({@link generic:use-a-theme-in-an-app}), and customize with `extends`. When the theme uses a custom font, name the families and the optional exported font stylesheet that `theme add` imports ({@link generic:fonts-and-assets}). Extend `theme` rather than a topic another package replaces, or an app that loads that package after yours drops your section.

Do not put theme usage in `agentDocs`. Agent lines land in every app's agent file and are for guidance needed every session; a theme's install-and-use steps belong in a doc topic that people and agents read on demand. See {@link generic:agent-guidance}.

docs.name: experimental
docs.title: Experimental features
docs.summary: Features you can try now that may change or be removed in a patch release.

blocks.text: Everything here is experimental: its commands (under `astryx experimental`), configuration (under `experimental` in astryx.config and in an integration manifest), output, and docs may change or be removed in any patch release, with no deprecation period. Nothing here changes what the rest of Astryx does unless you use it. A feature leaves this section when it becomes stable.

docs.name: export-template-assets
docs.title: Export the template and assets
docs.description: Make sure the published package contains and exposes everything the copied template imports.

content.text: `integration verify` resolves each template through a public package path without a file extension, such as `./templates/acme-dashboard`, and fails when that path is missing.

content.label: package.json

items: `integration add` writes this entry when `package.json` has an `exports` map ({@link generic:start-a-template}). Without a map it writes nothing, because creating one would make existing deep imports private. Add the map yourself, then the entry.
Keep the public path without `.tsx`. Only the target file ends in `.tsx`.
Do not point the entry at a barrel file that loses the template default export.

content.text: Add a public path for every package-owned component, helper, icon, or stylesheet that the copied source imports. Keep implementation-only files private.

content.label: Relevant package.json entries

content.text: If a block is also loaded directly as a live `.tsx` preview, add a pattern that keeps the extension, such as `"./templates/*.tsx": "./templates/*.tsx"`. Keep the generated entry too; `integration verify` resolves the template through it.
An export can point to a file that npm leaves out. When `package.json#files` exists, list the integration manifest, the templates directory, and every directory the copied file depends on.

content.label: package.json
content.code:
{
  "files": [
    "astryx.integration.mjs",
    "templates",
    "components",
    "icons",
    "styles",
    "assets/fonts"
  ],
  "sideEffects": ["**/*.css"]
}

items: `integration add` appends the manifest and templates directory when a `files` list already exists. Add the other directories yourself.
If `package.json` sets `sideEffects`, include CSS in it, as above, so bundlers keep side-effect stylesheet imports.
Run `{@pm-only npm "the tarball the registry receives" pack --dry-run}` and read the real file list instead of reasoning from the workspace.

sections.title: Declare what the copied file imports

content.text: A copied file imports from the app, so the app must install every package it imports. Declare the Astryx peers as described in {@link generic:versioning}. For other packages:

rows: Libraries the copied source imports, such as an icon library. List them in `devDependencies` too, so the package itself builds.
Runtime packages used only by package-owned modules, which should travel with the integration
Everything needed to build and test the integration itself

content.text: Use only ranges you test. A package that resolves only because a workspace hoisted it is not declared.

docs.name: extend-or-replace
docs.title: Extend or replace a topic
docs.description: Take over a topic or guide, or merge sections into it.

content.text: Set `replaces` to take over an existing topic, such as Core's `getting-started`. Readers who open the old name get your topic.

content.label: docs/acme-getting-started.doc.mjs

content.text: The docs list shows your topic in place of the old one. Because your topic has its own `name`, the old name keeps resolving to it, so links and agents that learned the old name still land on your topic.
Set `extends` to merge sections into an existing topic instead of owning it. A section replaces the base section it matches, and a section that matches none is added at the end.

content.code:
{@command integration add doc acme-theming --extends theme}
{@command docs theme --index}

content.label: docs/acme-theming.doc.mjs

items: Read the base topic's keys with `--index`, and give a section that replaces one that key as its `id`. A section that replaces one keeps its place. A section without an `id` matches only a base section with exactly its title, or one whose `id` is the key its title makes, so `Integration Themes` is added beside a base `Integration themes` that has no `id`.

Set `before` or `after` to a base section's key to add a new section there instead of at the end. A key that names no section adds it at the end, and `astryx doctor integration validate` lists a note. An older CLI rejects these fields, so declare an `@astryxdesign/cli` peer range that starts at the release that reads them; `astryx integration verify` warns without it.
The topic keeps the base's title and description, and readers open it by the base's name.
Replace the `Overview` placeholder that `integration add` writes, or it is added to the base topic.
Extend a topic to correct or add to it. A copy made with `replaces` stops getting the owner's fixes.

sections.title: Replace or extend a CLI guide

content.text: A guide in the CLI's docs tree has a route rather than a topic name. Set `replaces` or `extends` to that route to change the guide for every app that installs your package: say what differs for your users on the page agents already read.

content.label: docs/acme-quick-start.doc.mjs

items: Your doc stays a flat topic: do not give it a `placement`. Readers open the guide by its route, never by your `name`.
With `replaces`, readers of the route get your doc, under your package. With `extends`, each section you add or replace names your package.
A name that holds no topic or guide, such as a namespace, changes nothing; `astryx doctor integration validate` lists it as a note, with the guides below a namespace.

content.code:
# Every guide route, by namespace
astryx docs authoring --depth all
astryx docs cli --depth all
# The keys to place sections by
astryx docs authoring/quick-start --index

content.text: A topic sets `replaces` or `extends`, never both, and a placed guide sets neither. A topic that uses a Core topic's name with neither is an accidental conflict: apps keep reading the Core topic.

content.code: {@command doctor integration docs}

severity:     [info]
topic:        acme-getting-started
relationship: replaces
coreTopic:    getting-started
message:      Intentional override: "acme-getting-started" replaces the Core topic "getting-started".

severity:     [fail]
topic:        color
relationship: accidental
coreTopic:    color
message:      Accidental conflict: "color" is already a Core topic. Rename it, declare replaces: 'color' to take it over, or declare extends: 'color' to merge sections.

items: An intentional overlap prints as `[info]`. An accidental one fails with exit code 1.
A topic that sets both fails as `invalid_doc`, and so does a placed guide that sets either one.

content.text: In global mode: a doc that extends or replaces a topic from a package installed for the computer applies in folders outside any project; inside a project, only those from packages the project installs apply. See {@link namespace:global} and {@link generic:global-integrations}.

docs.name: field-reference
docs.title: Field reference
docs.description: Every file an integration author writes, field by field: the integration manifest, astryx.config, codemods, identity, and each doc type. The guides that use them are the rest of {@link namespace:authoring}.

content.text: The astryx.integration.* manifest that sits beside an integration package's package.json. It can preserve a stable provider identity across a package rename, and points the CLI at the package's components, templates, codemods, doc topics, source themes, managed agent guidance, issue tracker, and the command its users run the CLI with. Every field is optional.
Applies to: astryx.integration.{ts,mjs,js}

rows: The name that marks this package as the source of everything it contributes. Leave it out to use the package name from package.json. Set it to the old name only during a rename, so the IDs of what the package already contributed stay the same. If two packages use the same name here, the one you are working on wins; otherwise the one the CLI reads first wins, and the CLI warns about the other. Example: '@acme/widgets'.
The folder that holds your components and their docs, relative to package.json. Example: './src/components'.
The folder that holds your templates, relative to package.json. Example: './src/templates'.
The folder that holds your codemods, relative to package.json. Example: './codemods'.

The folder that holds your doc topics, relative to package.json. Every {topic}.doc.{ts,mjs,js} under it shows up in `{@command docs}`: a flat topic next to the built-in topics, where it can set `replaces` or `extends` to take over a built-in topic or add to it, and a guide with `placement` at its own route in the docs tree, under a namespace doc of the same package. Example: './docs'.

The folder that holds your themes, relative to package.json, with one folder per theme. Each theme folder has the theme source and a matching .doc.mjs file with the same name. Installed themes show up in `{@command theme list}`; `theme add` imports their built package exports, and `theme eject` creates an editable local fork. Example: './themes'.

Lines of guidance your package adds to the end of the agent instructions the CLI manages. The CLI owns the heading, labels, bullets, and which files it writes. Example: { append: ['Run acme verify.'] }.

Where people file issues for this package: an absolute URL, such as its GitHub issues page. A value that is not a URL fails the whole manifest; the scheme is not checked. Nothing warns when it is missing, but without it `{@command gap-report}` about this package fails unless the project or a loaded integration has a gapReport handler, and `{@command swizzle}` prints no feedback link for this package's components. When no handler is loaded, a github.com issues URL is filed with the GitHub CLI once the reporter passes `--confirm-public`; any other URL is returned for the reporter to open. Example: 'https://github.com/acme/widgets/issues'.
Link to this integration's docs site, such as its home page. Catalogs that list the package may show it. Example: 'https://widgets.acme.dev'.

The command your users run the Astryx CLI with, when it is not their package manager, such as a wrapper your company ships. Every command the CLI prints in an app that loads your package starts with it, in place of `pnpm exec astryx` or `yarn astryx`: hints, errors, Doctor fixes, and doc text. One line, without a subcommand. If two loaded packages set different commands, neither is used and `{@command doctor}` warns. An invalid value is ignored with an `invalid_cli_command` warning, and the rest of the manifest still loads. JSON output keeps commands bare. Example: 'acme astryx'.

content.label: Typical

content.text: In global mode: a manifest loads the same way when users install your package for their computer, beside the global CLI, and then applies in folders outside any project; inside a project, only if the project installs it. Peer ranges for `@astryxdesign/core` and `@astryxdesign/cli` are checked against the global CLI's release. See {@link namespace:global} and {@link generic:global-integrations}.

The provider name defaults to the package name in package.json. During a rename, set `providerId` to the old package name so the IDs of what the package already contributed stay the same. The package version always comes from package.json.

`agentDocs.append` may contain at most eight lines. Each line is a trimmed, non-blank string of at most 240 Unicode code points with no line separators, control characters, NUL, or Astryx/XDS managed-marker text. The configured project may contain at most 32 integration lines total. Write each command in a line as a bare `astryx` command; the managed block says once, before your lines, how the app starts the CLI.

Set `cliCommand` only when your users run the CLI with a command other than their package manager's, such as `acme astryx`. The CLI picks the command it prints in this order: the `cliCommand` of the loaded integrations when they name one command, then the command a host tool names, then the package manager's. Two different `cliCommand` values cancel out, and `{@command doctor}` warns in its `cli-command` check. See `{@command docs authoring/building-blocks/configuration/cli-command}`.

A themes root is version-gated: an older CLI lists and adds none of its themes. Depending on its age, that CLI ignores `themes` with an `unknown_manifest_key` warning and loads every other contribution kind, reports the root as invalid because it expects the earlier `manifest.json` theme catalog, or, if it is old enough to treat an unknown field as an error, rejects the whole manifest, so the package contributes nothing there.

Validate the manifest with `{@command doctor integration validate}`. At the load boundary, a known field of the wrong type is an error, issuesUrl and docsiteUrl must be valid URLs, and unknown fields become warnings so an older CLI can still load the fields it understands. Before publishing, also run `templates`, `components`, and `docs` under the same `doctor integration` group. Those leaves compare authored identities with Core and explain whether an overlap is intentional or needs a rename.

The optional astryx.config.* file at your project root. Declares which integrations to load, where to route issue links, post-codemod hooks, local debug-log and gap-report handlers, a discover source, and experimental layout components. All optional; {} is valid.
Applies to: astryx.config.{ts,mjs,js}

rows: Package names of Astryx integrations to load alongside core. Example: ['@acme/astryx-widgets'].

Where reports about Core go: `{@command gap-report}` routes a Core report here when no handler is loaded, gapReport handlers receive it as `report.target.issuesUrl`, and `{@command swizzle}` prints it as the feedback link for a Core component. A report or swizzle for an integration's component uses that integration's own issuesUrl, never this one. An absolute URL; a value that is not a URL makes the config invalid. Default: 'https://github.com/meta/astryx/issues/new'.

Commands to run after `{@command upgrade}` changes files (e.g. re-run your formatter). Each hook is an object `{name?, buildCommand}`: buildCommand gets `{packageDir, files}` and returns `{command, args?, options?}` to run, or null to skip. A dry run prints each command instead of running it.

Record every command run. The handler is synchronous; promises are not awaited and output goes to stderr. Declare `debug` directly in this file so early commands can discover it. An integration can supply one too, as a `debug` named export from its manifest. Every handler runs: yours first, then each integration's in load order (the `integrations` list, then autolinked ones). A handler that throws is skipped; the others still run and the command's result does not change. Set `{"astryx": {"inheritDebug": false}}` in package.json to take only your own. Example: event => appendFileSync('runs.ndjson', JSON.stringify(event) + '\n').

Handle explicit gap reports in addition to every loaded integration handler. The project handler runs first. Public handlers require caller consent; internal handlers always run. Example: { audience: 'internal', async handle(report, {signal}) { return sendGap(report, {signal}); } }.

Tell `{@command discover}` which integrations this project could add: an async function that returns a catalog. An integration can provide one too, as a `discover` named export from its manifest. Discover calls every source, yours first, and one that fails never hides the others. Discover only reads; your package manager installs. Example: async ({signal, package: name, version}) => fetchCatalog({signal, name, version}).
Unstable features; may change without a breaking bump.
Custom components for the removed layout expander, keyed by component name. The CLI still validates the field, so an entry without a string `from` makes `astryx.config` invalid, but nothing reads it.

content.label: Minimal
Send every command run somewhere of your own

content.text: The config is validated at load with a strict schema: an unknown key, a misspelled one included, or a value of the wrong type makes the whole file invalid. `{@command gap-report}`, `{@command discover}`, and `{@command upgrade}` stop with the error, and `{@command doctor}` fails its `config` check (exit 1). Reads such as `component`, `docs`, `search`, `template`, and `theme` carry on silently as if there were no config and no integrations, and no debug handler runs, so run `{@command doctor}` after editing the file.

One recorded CLI run: what a `debug` handler receives, whether it is set in astryx.config or exported by an integration manifest. There is exactly one event per run, and every field is present by the time a handler sees it.
Applies to: The argument of a `debug` handler

rows: Version of the recorded shape: 1, 2, or 3. A field that changes meaning gets a new version, so switch on this.
Unique per run. Deduplicate on it.
When the run started, as ISO 8601.
When the run ended, as ISO 8601.
How long the run took, in milliseconds.
The full command name. Empty when astryx ran without a command. Example: 'theme build'.
The command name split into segments. Example: ['theme', 'build'].
The arguments after the binary, scrubbed.
Positional arguments, keyed by their declared names.
The command options, as the CLI resolved them.
Where each option value came from: 'cli', 'default', 'env', 'config', or 'implied'. The keys match `options`.
The root flags, such as --json, --detail, and --lang.
The process exit code. When a signal ended the run, 128 plus the signal number.
The signal that ended the run, such as 'SIGINT'. Null otherwise.
The failure: `name`, `message`, `code`, and `stack`. Branch on `code`, never on `message`. Null when nothing failed.
What the run answered with: JSON mode, the envelope types, the result count and kind, and the stdout and stderr it printed, scrubbed and cut at the capture limit.
Runtime facts: the CLI and Node versions, platform, CI, package manager, and whether a person, an AI agent, or automation ran the command. It never holds a hostname, a user name, or a raw session ID.
The project the command ran in, as flags and counts. It never holds package names.
Whether the values in the record were scrubbed. It is true on every event a handler receives. When it is false, treat the log as sensitive.

content.label: Keep a local log of the runs that failed

content.text: The shape only grows: fields are added, never removed or given a new meaning. When a meaning must change, `schemaVersion` gets a new value. In version 3, a null `output.resultKind` means the run never reached an answer, so do not count it together with a version 1 or 2 null.
The handler runs synchronously as the process exits, so a promise it returns is never awaited. It gets a copy of the event, and anything it throws is ignored.
Import DebugEventOutput, DebugEventEnv, DebugEventProject, and DebugEventError from @astryxdesign/cli/authoring for the fields of `output`, `env`, `project`, and `error`.

A handler for `{@command gap-report}`: a plain object with an `audience` and a `handle` function. Set it as `gapReport` in astryx.config, or export it as `gapReport` from an integration manifest. Handlers add up rather than replace each other: the project handler first, then each loaded integration's in load order (the `integrations` list, then autolinked ones), whichever package the report is about.
Applies to: `gapReport` in astryx.config.*, or the `gapReport` named export of astryx.integration.*

rows: Whether the destination is internal to your organization or public. A public handler runs only when the caller agrees; an internal handler always runs.
Gets the report and returns a receipt. It can be async, and the CLI waits at most 30 seconds for it. A throw, a timeout, or an invalid receipt is a failed delivery, and the other handlers still run.
The report. Each handler gets its own copy.
The component the gap is about.
A readable name for the category.
What the caller was trying to do.
More detail, when the caller gave some.
When the report was sent, as ISO 8601.
The package the report is about.
The integration's version from its package.json. Null for Core, and when the package.json has none.
Where the package takes issues. Null when it does not say.
Aborted when the handler runs past 30 seconds.

content.label: A project handler in astryx.config

rows: 'filed': the handler created or queued the report. 'routed_only': it points to a place to file the report, and must return `url`. 'skipped': it chose not to act, for example on a duplicate.
An http or https URL. Required when status is routed_only.
A readable message of at most 2000 characters.

content.text: The receipt is strict: an unknown field, a URL that is not http or https, or a filed or routed_only receipt with neither `url` nor `message` is invalid.

A source for `{@command discover}`: an async function that returns a catalog of packages a project could add, their versions, and what each version adds. Set it as `discover` in astryx.config, or export it as `discover` from an integration manifest. Discover calls every source, the project one first, and then reads the official list the CLI carries; another source's entry for an official package is kept. A source that throws, runs past 30 seconds, or returns an invalid catalog never hides the others; discover then uses the last good answer that source gave for the same request, or reports the source as failed when it saved none. Discover only reads: it prints the command that adds a package and never runs it.
Applies to: `discover` in astryx.config.*, or the `discover` named export of astryx.integration.*

rows: The one argument the source is called with.
Aborted when the source runs past 30 seconds.
Set when discover shows one package: return that package with every version.
With `package`: return that version's contributions. Without it, the latest release's.
The catalog. Discover checks it, ignores fields and item kinds it does not know, and refuses any schemaVersion but 1.
Who answered, when the data was produced (ISO 8601), and false when the source knows its list is partial.
One entry per npm package. When two sources list the same package, the earlier source wins.
Shared by every npm name that publishes the same integration. Discover lists an integration once.
The integration's other npm names. Discover never offers a package the project has under another name.
One line, for the list and search.
The latest release. Null when there are only prereleases.
Every version, newest first: `{version, publishedAt, prerelease, status}`, where status is `ok` or why the version could not be read.

What the requested (else latest) version adds: `{kind, name, title?, summary?, keywords?}`, where kind is `component`, `template`, `doc`, `theme`, `codemod`, or `agent-doc` (a DiscoverKind) and name is the name the CLI uses for it.

content.label: A project source in astryx.config

content.text: In global mode: the discover source of an integration installed for the computer is called in folders outside any project; inside a project, only the sources of integrations the project installs are. See {@link namespace:global} and {@link generic:global-integrations}.

A codemod module the CLI runs during `{@command upgrade}`. Default-export a plain object with a `type` discriminant: 'code' rewrites source files, 'config' rewrites the astryx.config.* file. There is no factory to call.

Applies to: `<codemods>/<version>/<id>.{ts,mjs,js}` in an integration package: `<codemods>` is the codemods root of astryx.integration.*, and `<version>` is the exact @astryxdesign/core version (such as 0.7.0) whose upgrade runs the codemod. A file directly in the root never runs.

rows: Short, human-readable title shown in upgrade output. Example: 'Rename Button prop kind to variant'.
When true, the codemod runs only when explicitly requested. Default: false.
File extensions this codemod applies to. Code codemods only; a config codemod always targets astryx.config.*. Default: ['.tsx', '.ts', '.jsx', '.js', '.mjs', '.cjs']. Example: ['.tsx', '.ts'].
(file: AstryxCodemodFile, api: AstryxCodemodApi) => string | null | undefined
The transform. Return the new source to rewrite the file, or null/undefined to leave it unchanged.
The source file presented to the transform.
Absolute path to the file being transformed.
The current source contents of the file.
Helpers and context passed as the second argument.
A jscodeshift instance configured with a parser for the file.
Accepted for jscodeshift parity. A call does nothing, and upgrade shows nothing for it.
Accepted for jscodeshift parity. A call does nothing, and upgrade shows nothing for it.
Discriminant for the file-transforming variant. Use 'config' for a codemod that rewrites astryx.config.* instead (see notes). Example: 'code'.

content.label: Code codemod (type: code)
Config codemod (type: config)

content.text: The config-codemod variant (type: 'config') carries the same fields as a code codemod except fileExtensions: it always targets the astryx.config.* file rather than a set of source files.

Authors write a plain object and default-export it with the `type` discriminant; there is no factory. The CLI validates it at the load boundary via parseCodemod with a strict schema, and isOptional defaults to false.

Separates stable provider/artifact identity from package instances and runtime lifecycle state. Provider identity names integration manifests and settles provider conflicts. Docs-tree nodes are identified by doc identity; the tree covers the CLI's docs and each integration's. Artifact IDs for kinds outside the docs tree, provider instances, and compiler-input entries are defined for every provider-owned artifact; no command builds them.
Applies to: Integration manifests, provider conflicts, and docs-tree node ids.

rows: Canonical logical provider ID. It defaults to the lowercase npm package name; Core uses the same model without publishing an integration manifest.
Versioned serialization of provider ID, contribution kind, and stable artifact name. Every segment uses RFC 3986 escaping.
Artifact ID restricted to one authored doc kind. Navigation changes do not change it.
One immutable package version and source/content digest. It carries no installed, configured, loaded, selected, or healthy state.
{ id; provider; kind; stableName; source; authored }

Normalized compiler input. `stableName`, the key in its doc ID, is given separately from the authored display name; source paths remain package-relative, and provider provenance plus the authored snapshot are immutable.

content.text: Provider package renames require an explicit mapping: a ProviderInstance may retain its stable providerId while packageName changes. Silent identity changes are not inferred.

Fields every authored doc kind can declare for the docs tree: `placement`, `stability`, and two reserved fields, `aliases` and `audience`. The docs tree reads `placement` for every guide and namespace doc, the CLI's and each integration's. Nothing reads `aliases` or `audience` today: a reference topic that sets one fails to load, placed in the docs tree or not, and other doc kinds accept them and ignore them.
Applies to: Every authored doc kind's .doc.mjs object. Theme descriptors take none of these fields.

rows: Names the doc's one parent in the docs tree: a namespace of the same package, one of its slots, and an order. Read for every guide, the CLI's and each integration's, and for every namespace doc: a guide with `placement` gets a route in the tree instead of a flat topic name, and cannot also set `replaces` or `extends`; a namespace doc with `placement` nests under that parent. In the CLI's own topic directory a topic that sets it fails to load: the CLI keeps its guides in its docs tree directory. Commands, API functions, schemas, and enums do not set it: the tree adopts each by its `namespace`.
The parent namespace: `namespace:<name>` in the same package.
A slot the parent namespace declares; it must accept this doc's kind. Optional when the parent has one slot.
Integer sibling order within the slot. Docs without an order come after the ordered ones, sorted by title. The same order sets each doc's Previous and Next links.
Reserved: prior names or routes the docs tree will keep resolving to this doc, without creating another identity. Nothing reads it today, and a topic that sets it fails to load.
Reserved: which docs bundle includes this doc ('public' when omitted). Nothing reads it today, and a topic that sets it fails to load. Default: 'public'.

Marks the doc of an experimental surface: one whose shape can still change, or disappear, in any patch release. A command's help shows it as `[experimental]`. The doc's own text still says so. Omit it for a stable surface.

content.text: Unknown fields: `component`, `function`, `generic`, `schema`, `command` and `enum` docs accept a field they do not know, and nothing reads it, so a doc written for a newer CLI still loads here. `page`, `block` and `namespace` docs refuse one, as do `theme` descriptors. Sections and content blocks refuse one in every doc.

The doc-type for a component directory's {Name}.doc.mjs. A discriminated union of SingleComponentDoc (props on the doc), MultiComponentDoc (a `components` array), and SubComponentDoc (a `subComponentOf` pointer). All three share the ComponentBaseDoc fields below; the variant is chosen by which of props / components / subComponentOf you set.
Applies to: {Name}.doc.mjs

rows: Doc-kind discriminant for the stamped default-export format. Optional: legacy `export const docs = {...}` docs omit it and the parser falls back to shape-sniffing.

Stable machine identity without the Astryx prefix, PascalCase. e.g. 'Button', 'TextInput', 'AppShell'. For an integration component it is the export apps import: the doc sits beside the file that exports it, and when that file exports nothing under its own name, `name` may name the export it does have. Change `displayName`, not `name`, to edit the visible label; registry URLs derive from this identity by default.
Human-readable display name with spaces between words ('AppShell' → 'App Shell'). Drives the docsite gallery and sidebar label.
Optional public registry identity. The converter derives a stable kebab-case slug from `name`; set `slug` only to override it, and keep prior relative paths in `aliases` after a published rename.
Exact public package specifier consumers use to import an integration-owned component. The packed-package gate resolves this specifier and verifies it exports the component name.

Integration components only: the exact `name` of the Core ComponentDoc this component takes over for unqualified lookup, so every app that loads the integration gets it from component detail, component lists, search, `swizzle <Name>`, and issue routing; `swizzle --list` keeps listing Core names. The Core original stays reachable with `--package @astryxdesign/core`. It takes effect only when the package's peer range starts at the release that applies it, `"@astryxdesign/cli": ">=0.6.7"` or later; with a lower range nothing changes and `doctor integration components` warns ({@link generic:replace-a-core-component}). Set it only to intentionally own a Core identity; give an alternative or variant its own name instead.

Marks a deprecated component: it keeps working and stays documented, labeled with what replaces it. `replacement` is the `name` of the documented component to use instead; `description` is the modernization route in a sentence or two. The docsite shows a Deprecated badge in the component's page header and index tile, labels its search result, and adds a notice that links the replacement; `astryx search` results and `astryx build` kit entries carry the field. Omit it for a component that is not deprecated.

Search keywords for CLI discovery: synonyms and related UI concepts from other design systems (MUI, Chakra, Radix, and others). Lowercase. `astryx search` matches them; `astryx component <term>` also suggests Core components by keyword.

Sub-component names to hide from human-facing UI (CLI listings, docs catalogs). They stay public and importable; agents and tooling can still discover them via source. In an integration it hides only full entries in this doc's `components`, which the CLI then neither lists nor opens; hide a sub-component that has its own doc with `hidden` in that doc.
Hide this entire component from human-facing UI. It stays public and importable. Use for a shared primitive that only makes sense inside its parent.
Optional sidebar/docs group. Clusters related components; ungrouped components appear flat in alphabetical order.
Overview-gallery category representing the component's functional role. Independent of `group` (which is for the sidebar). `Data Input` is a deprecated compatibility alias for `Form Controls`.
Exclude from the categorized overview page while keeping the component in the sidebar and CLI. Use for sub-components or internal primitives.
{ container?: boolean; targets: ComponentThemingTarget[]; vars?: ComponentThemingVar[]; derived?: ComponentThemingDerivedVar[]; componentIcons?: ComponentIconSlotDoc[] }
Theming configuration: the stable selector surface (astryx-* classes + data-attribute reflections) that themes target via @scope selectors in defineTheme.
Marks a container component. Nothing reads it today: the theme pipeline maps `padding` to container tokens from a `theming.derived` entry `{property: 'padding', expand: 'container'}`.
Selector targets rendered by this component. Each entry corresponds to a themeProps() call in the source.
CSS custom properties exposed for theming.

Maps standard CSS properties to internal vars for theme-pipeline expansion. Ordered by priority: earlier entries emit first. The pipeline reads only Core components' entries, so an integration's have no effect.

The component's icon slots, which a theme maps through `defineTheme({componentIcons})`: each slot's name, role, fallback per state, the state a slot function receives, and what `null` does. Each entry corresponds to a slot in `ComponentIconSlotMap`.

Component usage documentation: concise summary, best practices, component-specific accessibility requirements, and optional visual anatomy. Required on a component doc; optional on a sub-component doc (`subComponentOf`), which uses its description instead.
What the component is and when to use it, in 2-3 short sentences.
3-4 do/don't design-guidance items ({guidance: boolean, description: string}). Never start the description with 'Do' or 'Don't'.

Component-specific requirements rendered in the shared Accessibility tab. Write at about a grade-7 reading level with short sentences, common words, and active voice. For color contrast, put the ratio in `requirement`; name the exact foreground, background, state, and any overlay in `description`; explain exceptions in plain language; and give a human or agent enough detail to reproduce the check. Keep repository audit procedures in the wiki rubric.

Verified per-theme accessibility measurements rendered in the shared Accessibility tab. Record light and dark mode separately, include rendered color pairs, and mark failed measurements. Put visuals excluded from the audit in `notMeasured` with a short reason; do not add them as table measurements. Each theme declares `applicability` for measured values, informed by the component contract and never inferred from the ratio: `Conditional` is required only in some contexts, `Supplemental` adds another meaningful cue, and `Decorative` has no required meaning. These values do not change row status. Provide a complete breakdown when one cell summarizes multiple combinations, and protect derived values with an automated audit.
Structural/visual parts in reading order ({name, required, description}).
Short code examples ({label?, code}) rendered by the CLI after the props table.

Interactive-preview config: initial prop `defaults`, `overlay` for modal-only components, `appShellMobile` for components gated on AppShell mobile context, and a `wrapper` for context-dependent sub-components.

SingleComponentDoc variant (required there): all public props for the one primary component. Each prop is {name, type, description, default?, required?, slotElements?, stability?}. Skip styling props like xstyle/className/style. Also present on SubComponentDoc.

MultiComponentDoc variant (required there): one entry per public component/hook exported from the directory. Each entry is a full ComponentEntry (inline: name, displayName, description, props | params+returns) or a name-only ComponentRef pointing at a sibling {Name}.doc.mjs. In an integration, each full entry the module named by `import` exports is a component under its own name.

SubComponentDoc variant (required there): the parent component's `name` (e.g. 'Chat'). Marks this file as a sub-component doc. The CLI does not copy family fields (group, category, keywords, theming, playground) from the parent to an integration's sub-component: its detail, list group and search use only what its own doc sets. Set any the child needs in its own doc.

SubComponentDoc variant (required there): one-sentence description of the sub-component's role within the parent composition. Single/Multi docs have no top-level description; they derive their summary from `usage`.

content.label: SingleComponentDoc (props on the doc)
MultiComponentDoc (a components array)

content.text: When it loads, a stamped component doc is checked about as loosely as an unstamped one, so adding `type: 'component'` to a doc that follows the type never breaks it: `displayName` may be missing, `category` may be any string, `usage`, `theming` and `playground` are not checked, and `examples` need only be an array. Unlike an unstamped doc, each entry in a group doc's `components` must have a `name`, and `import` and `replaces`, when set, must be non-empty strings. Write to the type anyway; it is the contract.
ComponentDoc is a discriminated union of three shapes that all extend ComponentBaseDoc. Pick the variant by which key you set: `props` (single), `components` (multi), or `subComponentOf` (sub).

items: SingleComponentDoc: one primary component; put props directly on the doc via `props`. Use for Switch, Badge, Spinner, TextInput.
MultiComponentDoc: a directory exporting several components/hooks; list them in `components` (inline ComponentEntry or name-only ComponentRef). Use for Table, Dialog, TabList.

SubComponentDoc: a single sub-component in its own {Name}.doc.mjs inside the parent directory; set `subComponentOf` to the parent name. It does not take the parent's family fields, and it may omit `usage`.

content.label: SubComponentDoc

content.text: The stamped format is `export default { type: 'component', ... }`, which `astryx integration add component` writes; legacy docs use `export const docs = {...}` and omit `type` (the parser shape-sniffs). A hook that is part of a component API is listed in a MultiComponentDoc `components` array: inline as a ComponentEntry (with `params`/`returns`), or by name with its own SubComponentDoc file, as Core's useTableSelection is.

The doc-type for a standalone React hook (e.g. useMediaQuery, useFocusTrap, useOverflow) that gets its own `.doc.mjs`. Hooks that are part of a component API (e.g. useImperativeDialog) belong in that component's MultiComponentDoc `components` array instead. `HookDoc` is the hook-flavored view of the shared `type: 'function'` kind. `astryx hook` reads Core's hook docs only; an integration lists its hooks in a component doc's `components` array.
Applies to: {useX}.doc.mjs

rows: Doc-kind discriminant (shared with FunctionDoc). Legacy `export const docs = {...}` docs omit it.
Stable hook name exactly as exported, e.g. 'useMediaQuery', 'useFocusTrap'. Change `displayName`, not `name`, to edit the visible label; registry URLs derive from this identity by default.
Human-readable display name. Hooks read better as the raw identifier ('useMediaQuery') than spaced, so keep the identifier verbatim.
Optional public registry identity. The converter derives a stable kebab-case slug from `name`; set `slug` only to override it, and keep prior relative paths in `aliases` after a published rename.
Optional group for sidebar/docs organization; same as ComponentDoc.group.
TypeScript type signature as a string.
Default value as a string, if optional with a default.
True if required. Omit if optional.
Return value documentation. For object returns, list each field; for primitive returns, use a single entry.
Field name on the returned object, or 'value' for primitive returns.
Usage documentation: description and best practices.
What the hook is and when to use it, in 2-3 short sentences.
3-4 do/don't design-guidance items ({guidance: boolean, description: string}).
Accessibility requirements specific to using the hook ({name, description}).
Structural/visual anatomy elements (rarely used for hooks).
Component names this hook is commonly used with. Enables cross-referencing (e.g. `astryx hook useToast` links back to Toast).
Other hook names this hook is commonly used with.

content.label: A standalone hook doc

content.text: `parseDoc` accepts a stamped hook doc without `displayName` and does not check its `usage`, and `astryx hook` prints a hook doc without checking it at all. Write to the type anyway; it is the contract.
A hook's discriminant is `type: 'function'`: HookDoc and FunctionDoc share the generalized function kind. HookDoc is the hook-flavored view: named `returns` fields and a required `usage` block.

A hook that is part of a component API is listed in that component's MultiComponentDoc `components` array: inline with `params`/`returns`, or by name with its own SubComponentDoc file, as Core's useTableSelection is.

The generalized `type: 'function'` doc-type covering both React hooks and CLI/API functions. A hook (HookDoc) is the hook-flavored view of this same kind; FunctionDoc adds the fields an API function needs (a {type, data} return envelope, thrown error codes, the wrapping CLI command). The CLI binding itself lives in a separate CommandDoc.
Applies to: api/<dir>/<name>.doc.mjs

rows: Which flavor. Nothing reads it today: no reader sections docs by it or infers it from `importPath`. The CLI's API function docs set 'api'.

Optional in the type, but every doc the CLI ships declares it. The group that reads this doc. The CLI's API functions use 'cli/api', which the docs tree adopts by kind: each is the leaf `cli/api/functions/<name>`, the name in kebab case (`themeUse` is `theme-use`). Every function doc the CLI ships declares one, and `astryx doctor` fails on one that is missing or that nothing reads.
Reserved: other names for this doc. Nothing reads it today, so they do not resolve to it.
Full signature as a string, e.g. 'search(query, options?): Promise<SearchResponse>'.
TypeScript type signature as a string.
Default value as a string, if optional with a default.
True if required. Omit if optional.
Return documentation. Hooks list named return fields (`name` set); API functions list {type, data} envelope entries where `type` is the response discriminant and `name` is omitted.
Field name (hooks); omit for API envelope entries.
TS type (hooks) or response-type discriminant (API), as a string.
What this return value / envelope entry provides.
Errors the function throws (API functions), keyed to ERROR_CODES.
The condition under which it is thrown.
Optional heading shown above the snippet.
Usage documentation (hooks): description, best practices, accessibility requirements, and anatomy. Same shape as HookDoc.usage.
The CLI command that wraps this function, e.g. 'search'.
Related function names; the CLI links each to its doc. Name the CLI command with `command`, not here.
Component names this is commonly used with (hooks).
Other hook names this is commonly used with (hooks).

content.label: An API function doc (envelope return, no field name)

content.text: `parseDoc` accepts a stamped function doc without `displayName` and does not check its `usage`, and the CLI reads its own function docs without checking them. Write to the type anyway; it is the contract.
The `type` discriminant is 'function' for both flavors. `kind: 'hook'` or `kind: 'api'` names the flavor; nothing reads it today.

The two flavors differ in `returns`: a hook lists named fields (`name` set), while an API function lists {type, data} envelope entries whose `type` is the response discriminant and whose `name` is omitted. `throws` (keyed to ERROR_CODES) applies to API functions.

The function does not know it has a CLI. The terminal binding (args, flags, exit codes) lives in a separate CommandDoc that references this function via `fn`; here you only note the wrapping command name via `command`.

The doc-type for a CLI command: the terminal binding of an operation. A command is not its own behavior; it is a FunctionDoc exposed on the CLI, referenced via `fn`, carrying only CLI-surface facts (args, flags, subcommands, examples, exit codes). A `defineCommand` converter turns it into Commander config + `--help`.
Applies to: clients/cli/commands/<name>.doc.mjs

rows: Doc-kind discriminant. Marks the file as a command doc.
One-line summary → Commander `.description()` + the docs listing.
Longer body / when-to-use. `astryx docs` prints it after the summary; `--help` shows only the summary.

Optional in the type, but every doc the CLI ships declares it. The group that reads this doc. The CLI's commands use 'cli/commands', which the docs tree adopts: each is the leaf `cli/commands/<name>`, spaces as hyphens (`theme build` is `cli/commands/theme-build`). Every command doc the CLI ships declares one, and `astryx doctor` fails on one that is missing or that nothing reads.
Reserved: other names for this doc. Nothing reads it today, so they do not resolve to it.
Name of the FunctionDoc (and `@astryxdesign/cli/api` export) this command wraps. Example: 'search'.
FunctionDoc param this arg binds to; `astryx docs` shows that param's description when the arg has none.
Override description. `--help` shows an argument's description only when it sets this.
Whether the positional argument must be supplied.
Whether the argument collects a variable number of values.
FunctionDoc param this flag maps to (inherits its description).
Override/explicit description. Nothing requires it: a flag with neither this nor `param` shows no description.
Default value: a string, a boolean, or a list of strings.
True for CLI-only flags with no function param (e.g. --verbose). Nothing reads it.
Optional heading shown above the invocation.
A full terminal invocation, e.g. 'astryx search button --json'.
The condition that produces this exit code.

What the command does outside a project. `same`: the answer it gives in a new project. `refuse`: it writes nothing and fails, naming the app project or integration package it needs. `own`: something else. Every `refuse` and `own` command also carries an `In global mode:` note in its `notes` that tells readers exactly what it does. Every command and subcommand declares one, and `astryx manifest` publishes it; a command that only groups subcommands declares none. The CLI tests run every command in an empty folder and check what it does against this value; `astryx doctor` does not check it.
Deprecation notice — a DEP-* id and the replacement.

content.label: A command that wraps the search() function

content.text: A command carries only CLI-surface facts. Behavior, parameters, returns, and thrown errors live in the FunctionDoc it points at via `fn`; the function does not know it has a CLI.

Bind an arg/option to a function param via `param` so it inherits that param's description: an option's in `--help` and `astryx docs`, an arg's in `astryx docs` only. Mark a flag with no function param (e.g. `--verbose`) `cliOnly: true` and give it its own `description`; nothing checks either. `--json` is a global flag, so a command doc does not declare it.

The doc-type for a closed vocabulary: a fixed set of literal values such as error codes or response-type discriminants. Colocated as a `.doc.mjs` next to the source of truth it documents. Only the CLI reads enum docs, from its own source: one in an integration's docs directory fails to load, and so do that package's other docs.
Applies to: <enum>.doc.mjs

rows: Doc-kind discriminant. Optional in the type, but the CLI reads a doc as an enum doc only when it is set; without it the doc drops out of the docs tree.
URL-safe identifier, used as the docs slug within its namespace. Example: 'error-codes'.

Optional in the type, but every doc the CLI ships declares it. The group that reads this doc. The CLI's enums use 'cli/api', which the docs tree adopts by kind: each is the leaf `cli/api/enums/<name>`. Every enum doc the CLI ships declares one, and `astryx doctor` fails on one that is missing or that nothing reads.
Reserved: alternate slugs for this doc. Nothing reads it today, so `astryx docs <alias>` does not open it.
The enumerated members: one entry per literal value.
What the value means / when it occurs.

content.label: Error-codes enum doc

content.text: An enum doc is the human-readable mirror of a closed vocabulary defined elsewhere in source (e.g. an ERROR_CODES map or a response-type union). Keep the members in sync with that source of truth.
Mark a value with `deprecated` (a migration hint) rather than deleting it, so old codes stay documented while readers are pointed at the replacement.

Declares one level of the docs tree: named slots, and adoption rules for already-discovered docs. It never scans folders, lists its children, or copies child documents: a child names its parent with `placement`, or a namespace adopts a discovery group. `astryx docs <route>` lists each slot's children one level down. The CLI keeps its namespace docs in its docs tree directory; an integration ships its own in its docs directory, and they appear in `astryx docs` beside the CLI's.
Applies to: <namespace>.doc.mjs

rows: Stable provider-local identity. Moving the namespace does not change this value.
One-line summary used in listings and search results.

Optional canonical parent: {parent, slot?, order?}. `parent` names a namespace of the same package as `namespace:<name>`. An invalid placement withdraws the namespace with a diagnostic; it never falls back.
Prior names or routes the docs tree will keep resolving to this doc. Not read yet.
Reserved: bundle audience. Nothing reads it yet: a namespace that sets 'internal' still shows in `astryx docs`. Default: 'public'.
Search terms not already present in the title or summary.
Named placement and collection targets. Each slot declares a title and the doc kinds it accepts. `accepts.providers` is not read yet: only docs of the namespace's own package can be placed in a slot.
Provider-local rules that adopt otherwise-unplaced docs from a logical discovery group. They never scan a folder.

Ordered layout content for the namespace page. Graph-only workflow, collection, and reference blocks are available here without widening the stable ReferenceContentBlock union used by existing topic renderers. `astryx docs <route>` prints the prose, heading, code, table, and list blocks above the slots, and `--json` returns every block with its links resolved. A collection block is not rendered yet, and `astryx doctor` warns on one.

content.label: A CLI namespace with one adopted source group

content.text: The docs tree reads namespace docs from the CLI and from every configured integration. An integration's namespace doc without a `placement` is a top-level level of the tree, and its guides name it with `placement`; a doc can be placed only in a namespace of its own package. When two packages claim one route, the CLI's own docs win, then integrations in configured order, and `astryx doctor` names the loser.

Child docs request one canonical home with placement. A collection block refers to those docs by stable reference and never creates a second identity or parent. It is not rendered yet: `astryx doctor` warns on one.

items: Use a directory as implicit navigation.
Put JSX, HTML, ANSI, callbacks, or custom renderer code in a doc.
Use choice, callout, or checklist blocks before the full block-extension contract exists.

content.text: The doc-type for a reference/topic doc: tokens, principles, theming, patterns, accessibility, migration guides. Unlike ComponentDoc it is not tied to a component: drop a `.doc.mjs` in the docs directory and it shows up in `astryx docs`. Content is built from ordered sections of mixed content blocks.
Applies to: <topic>.doc.{ts,mjs,js} in the folder the integration manifest's `docs` names

rows: Doc-kind discriminant. Stays 'generic' (the reference/topic discriminant). Legacy `export const docs = {...}` docs omit it.
URL-safe identifier, used as the CLI topic name. e.g. 'tokens', 'principles'.
Human-readable title. e.g. 'All Tokens'. (Reference docs use `title`, not `displayName`.)
One-line summary shown in topic listings.

Words a reader may search for that the title and sections do not use: a synonym, a task, or another library's name for the same thing. `astryx search` matches each as a keyword of the whole topic, so an exact one ranks the topic like its own title does. Example: ['dark mode', 'color scheme'].

Name of an existing topic this doc takes the place of. Authored by an integration that serves its own guide instead of the built-in one: on a doc of the same name it swaps the content, and on a doc of another name it also leaves the old name as an alias so `astryx docs <old>` still resolves. Exclusive with `extends`. Example: 'getting-started'.

Name of an existing topic this doc merges onto, section by section. A section replaces the base section with the same `id`, or else the one with exactly its title when either of the two has no `id`. A key derived from a title counts only against an `id`: a section without an `id` also matches a base section whose `id` is the key its title derives, and a section with an `id` also matches a base section without one whose title derives that `id`. Two different `id`s never match, two sections without an `id` whose titles differ only in case or punctuation stay separate, and a section that matches none is appended. The topic keeps the base's title and description. For correcting or adding to a topic rather than owning it. Exclusive with `replaces`. Example: 'theme'.
Ordered sections that make up the doc. Each becomes an h2 in full output and can be retrieved via `astryx docs <topic> <section>`.

Stable section anchor. New docs should set this instead of relying on a mutable title. Published @astryxdesign/cli 0.6.3 and earlier reject the field and hide every doc topic the package ships, so `astryx integration verify` fails an integration that sets one until it declares an `@astryxdesign/cli` peer of `>=0.6.4`.
Navigation category ('guide' | 'foundations'). Mirrors the parent doc's category so sections can be grouped independently.

Ordered content blocks: prose, heading, code, table, list, token-ref, and reference. A `reference` block (`{type: 'reference', target, projection?, presentation?}`) includes another doc from its canonical source instead of a copy: a schema, command, function, or enum doc as `astryx docs` prints it, then the command that opens it. `projection.fields` keeps only those fields of a schema; `presentation` is `full` (the default), `compact` (no code blocks), or `summary` (only the doc's title, summary, and command). Any other doc shows as a summary. Graph-only workflow and collection blocks are available through GraphContentBlock on NamespaceDoc, without widening the stable ReferenceContentBlock union. Inside text, `{@link <target>}` links another doc by identity (`[<provider>:]<kind>:<name>`): the CLI prints the command that opens it, and `astryx doctor` warns on one that names no doc.
Preview type for token tables in this section. The CLI rejects a value not in the list below and returns the value in `astryx docs --json`, but draws no preview from it. Omit for non-token sections.
Token category for foundational docs that map to a token section (e.g. 'color'). `astryx docs --json` returns it as authored; no tokens page links to the doc through it.

content.label: A reference doc with one section

content.text: A stamped generic doc without `title`, `description` or `sections` still loads, as older codemod output does; its title falls back to `displayName` or `name`. Without a description and sections it is not a usable topic, and `astryx doctor` reports it.

Each `sections[].content` is an ordered array of ReferenceContentBlock, the stable discriminated union of prose, heading, code, table, list, and token-ref, plus the reference block (ReferenceDocBlock). A read inlines a reference block the way it inlines a token-ref, so `astryx docs`, in text and in `--json`, returns only the stable block kinds. Docs-graph-only workflow and collection blocks are exported separately as GraphContentBlock and accepted by NamespaceDoc. choice, callout, and checklist remain invalid. ReferenceContentBlock is also reused by the `notes` field on SchemaDoc and CommandDoc.
