docs.name: layout
docs.title: Layout
docs.summary: Build an app layout outside-in: scaffold the regions, structure the content, tune the spacing, then adapt across widths.

blocks.text: Build a layout outside-in. Settle the shell and its region budgets before any content exists, then work inward. Content-first layouts drift into a padded column of cards, because every section ends up inventing its own container.

items: Scaffold: pick the shell, budget each region, and choose navigation
Structure: rank each region's content and choose its container
Spacing: align each region to one content line, then set gaps and density
Breakpoints: decide what each region does as width changes

blocks.text: This guide decides layout, not component APIs. Run `{@command build "<idea>"}` to start from the closest template for your app type, and `{@command component <Name>}` for a component's props.

docs.name: layout-spacing
docs.title: Layout spacing
docs.description: Hold one content line per region, then tune gaps and density.

content.text: Hold one content line per region, then tune gaps and density. Alignment, Rhythm, and Density and size each build on these rules.

items: Let the container own padding; children zero their own margins
Hold one content line per region: text on the line, hover backgrounds bleed to the edge
Hold one padding token across a region header, body, and footer
Contrast tight and generous gaps so grouping reads without borders
One control size per row; match density to use frequency
Double padding: a component indented past its Section heading (keep one inset owner)
Raw px for interior spacing; tokens only, px is for structural widths
One repeated gap everywhere, which flattens grouping
Mixed control sizes in a single row

content.text: The container owns padding and child gaps; children zero their margins, and interior spacing is always a token. Pick one content line per region and hold it constant, not the padding: `container_inset = content_line - component_intrinsic_inset`.

items: Text and Heading carry no inset, so the container takes the full padding
List, Tab, Menu, and nav items carry a small inset, so the container gives up its padding and the component owns the line
Table cells carry a larger inset, so the container gives up its padding and the cell owns the line

content.label: One content line, two inset owners

content.text: Verify: draw one vertical line down the left of the region. Every label touches it; only hover and selected backgrounds cross it.
Grouping comes from contrast between tight and generous gaps, not one repeated value. If every gap is the same step, proximity does no work.

items: Tight gaps bind: the smallest steps, used inside an item or field
Generous gaps separate: several steps up, used between sections
Reach for the in-between steps to tune cadence, rather than rounding everything to the same two values

content.label: Tight inside, generous between
content.code:
// Tight binds at gap={1}–{2}, generous separates at gap={4}–{6}.
// In-between steps tune cadence: gap={3} = 12px, gap={5} = 20px.
<VStack gap={6}>
  <VStack gap={1}>
    <Text weight="semibold">Retention</Text>
    <Text color="secondary">Logs are kept for 30 days</Text>
  </VStack>
  <VStack gap={1}>{/* next label and value */}</VStack>
</VStack>

content.text: Verify: with every border removed, you can still name the groups from spacing alone. If you cannot, the intervals are too uniform. Form fields are the exception: FormLayout owns their spacing.
Match density to how often a region is used, and give every control in a row the same size so heights share a baseline.

items: Compact: high-volume regions scanned fast, like logs, monitors, and large datasets
Balanced: most Table and List surfaces
Spacious: low-frequency or high-stakes rows, like settings or a short selection list

content.label: Density paired with control size

content.text: Verify: every interactive element in a row shares one size, and that size is paired with the density of the region it sits in.

docs.name: links
docs.title: Links
docs.description: Link one doc to another so the link keeps working when the doc moves.

content.text: Write `{@link [provider:]kind:name}` in prose, list items, and table cells to link another doc. The CLI prints the command that opens it, so the link keeps working when the doc moves.

content.code:
{type: 'prose', text: 'Before you ship, read {@link generic:deploying}.'},
{type: 'list', style: 'unordered', items: ['All guides: {@link namespace:acme}.']},
{type: 'table', headers: ['Task', 'Guide'], rows: [['Ship', '{@link generic:deploying}']]},

items: The kind is `generic` for a topic or guide, `namespace` for a docs section, `command` or `function` for a CLI command or API function, `schema` or `enum` for a schema or a fixed set of values, `component` for a component, and `page` or `block` for a template.
Name a component by its export name and a template by its id. Its link reads as the command that opens it, such as `{@command component AcmeCarousel --package @acme/widgets}`.
Inside backticks or a code block, link syntax prints as written.

content.text: A link without a provider resolves against your own package. To link the CLI's docs, or another package's, start the target with that package's name, such as `@astryxdesign/cli:`.

items: Name a CLI command the way you type it, spaces included, such as `@astryxdesign/cli:command:doctor integration docs`.
In a topic that `extends` another package's topic, your sections still resolve against your package, so a link to the base topic's docs needs its provider.

sections.title: Fix a link that names no doc

content.text: A link that names no doc prints as written, and `doctor integration docs` warns. The warning names a search that finds the right target.

content.code: {@command doctor integration docs}

severity: [warn]
code:     invalid_doc_graph
message:  acme/deploying § check-before-you-ship: "command:doctor" names no doc. Find it with `astryx search doctor --type doc`, then name it as `[<provider>:]<kind>:<name>`.

items: The warning keeps exit code 0, so read the report before you ship; see {@link generic:check-your-docs}.
Published 0.6.4 and later read links. An older CLI, such as published 0.6.3, prints each one as written; see {@link generic:versioning}.

docs.name: migration
docs.title: Migration
docs.summary: Migrate an existing Tailwind, shadcn, or Radix app to the design system incrementally — setup, component replacement, and verification.

docs.name: migration-setup
docs.title: Setup
docs.description: Install the theme, wire CSS layers, audit resets, and run the foundation smoke test before migrating any surface.

content.text: Treat migration as a product-shell and workflow migration, not a global class replacement. Start by putting the app inside Theme and AppShell, then move one route or surface at a time to design system primitives while keeping existing data, routing, and business logic intact.

Tailwind can coexist during migration. Use it for legacy wrappers and local layout while replacing interactive controls, navigation, command surfaces, forms, alerts, dialogs, and settings UI with components.

items: Install the packages and run `{@command init}` for agent docs, then add the reset, `astryx.css`, and theme CSS imports (see Theme and CSS Setup below).
Wrap the app root with Theme and choose the initial light, dark, or system mode behavior.
Make Tailwind and design system CSS layer order explicit before replacing components.
Render the foundation smoke test page and confirm primitives keep their padding before migrating any surface.
Move the persistent frame first: AppShell, TopNav, SideNav, page content, and mobile navigation. See {@link generic:component-migration}.

Replace shared primitives: Button, IconButton, TextInput, NumberInput, Switch, CheckboxInput, RadioList, Selector, TabList, Dialog, AlertDialog, Banner, Toast, Badge, Card, Table, and ListItem. See {@link generic:component-migration}.
Replace global workflows: command palette, settings popover, theme toggle, search, filters, create flows, and destructive confirmation dialogs.
Remove legacy Tailwind classes from each completed surface, keeping only token-backed layout utilities or local wrappers that still need to be migrated.
Verify both light and dark modes, keyboard navigation, responsive layout, and empty/error/loading states before moving to the next route. See {@link generic:migration-verification}.

content.text: Use the CLI as the migration checklist. Read the docs for the pattern you are about to touch, inspect a matching template skeleton, then read the exact component docs before editing.

content.label: Migration-oriented CLI pass

content.text: For a shorter read to paste into an AI coding tool, see {@link generic:working-with-ai}. Use `--json` when building automated migration reports.

content.label: Short and JSON modes
content.code:
{@command docs migration --full --detail brief}
{@command component Button --json}

content.text: Mount Theme at the app root so every migrated component reads the same token set. Keep the mode in application state if users can switch between light and dark themes.

content.label: Root provider with explicit mode

content.text: When Tailwind remains in the app, declare layer order once in the global CSS file. Load the Astryx reset and theme CSS before Tailwind utilities so migrated components keep design system defaults while legacy utility classes still work. On Tailwind v4, use the imports and layer order in {@link generic:tailwind}.

Import the global CSS file first in the root layout or app entry, before anything that imports Astryx or theme CSS, including the `astryx-themes` module and a root component like the `AppRoot` above. Why the order matters, and what to do when it cannot come first, is in {@link generic:tailwind}.

content.label: Root layout or app entry
content.code:
import './globals.css'; // first: declares the cascade-layer order

import {AppRoot} from './AppRoot';

content.text: On Tailwind v3 there is no preflight.css to import, so wrap the @tailwind base directive in a named layer instead. Keep utilities unlayered so existing app utility classes still win everywhere. Put the `@layer` order line in its own `layers.css` and import it first, before `globals.css`: Next.js (webpack or Turbopack) and other bundlers that hoist CSS imports move the imported files above an inline `@layer` line, so the order would arrive too late.

content.label: layers.css (imported first)
content.code: @layer reset, tw-preflight, astryx-base, astryx-theme;

content.label: globals.css (Tailwind v3 coexistence)
Root layout or app entry (Tailwind v3)

content.text: In a stylesheet with no layers at all, a zero-specificity reset like `* { padding: 0 }` loses to any class selector, so most developers treat resets as harmless. Layers change the rules twice: unlayered styles beat every named layer, and a later layer beats an earlier one, both regardless of specificity. The same reset therefore wins against every component style either by staying unlayered or by landing in a layer declared after astryx-base. Same CSS, opposite outcome, and no error or warning when it happens.

This is the most common way an adoption breaks, through one of two @import mechanisms. A top-level @import without the layer() keyword keeps the legacy reset unlayered, where it overrides every design system layer. And an @import nested inside a file that was itself imported into a layer inherits that surrounding layer, so a reset can silently land in a consumer layer above astryx-base. Either way the fix is the same: import the legacy reset into the lowest layer explicitly.

content.label: Legacy reset, explicitly layered
content.code:
/* was: @import "./legacy-reset.css";  (unlayered: beats every layer) */
@import "./legacy-reset.css" layer(reset);

content.text: Before building screens, check every stylesheet against the cascade layer audit below.
Audit the layers around the design system with this checklist before building screens.

items: Declare the canonical @layer order once, before any @import. With Next.js (webpack or Turbopack) and other bundlers that hoist CSS imports, the order declaration must live in its own CSS file imported first, such as layers.css, because the bundler hoists @import content above the inline CSS that follows it.

Audit every pre-existing global or reset stylesheet and assign each one to a layer deliberately. Top-level imports without layer() stay unlayered and beat every layer; imports nested inside a layered file inherit that layer.
Remove or demote the app legacy reset. The design system ships its own :where() reset in the lowest layer, so any app reset belongs in that same reset layer and never in a layer above astryx-base.

Layer Tailwind preflight. On Tailwind v4, import preflight.css with layer(base). On Tailwind v3, wrap the @tailwind base directive in a named layer (see the snippet in Theme and CSS Setup). Unlayered preflight overrides theme CSS silently.
Set moduleResolution to bundler or node16 and newer so subpath imports like @astryxdesign/core/reset.css resolve.

Theme with defineTheme and the accent family API instead of hand-writing individual color tokens. Derived tokens like --color-on-accent are generated from the accent scale automatically; hand-writing only --color-accent leaves --color-on-accent at its stale white default with no contrast guarantee against the new accent.
Run the foundation smoke test below and view a few components in both light and dark mode before migrating any route.

content.text: One more mental model shift: a className or utility class you write on a component still reaches the DOM either way, but whether it overrides the component is a layer question, not a source order question. Keep app utilities in the utilities layer so they keep winning.

A broken layer order fails silently and identically on every page, so catch it before feature work instead of after N migrated screens. Render one throwaway page with a few primitives as the first migration step.

content.label: Foundation check page

content.text: If the button renders with visible padding, a filled primary background, and the input and card have borders and internal spacing, the foundation is sound. For an assertion that can run in any test runner or a dev-only effect, check that a primitive keeps non-zero padding:

content.label: Foundation assertion

content.text: When this fails, the fix is almost always in the layer order: find the stylesheet that zeroes padding, and move it into the reset layer or delete it.

docs.name: migration-verification
docs.title: Verification
docs.description: Post-migration verification checklist and an AI migration prompt to paste into your coding tool.

items: Run the app in light and dark mode and check that surfaces, borders, text, icons, hover states, focus rings, and status colors flow together.
Open the command palette from the shell, type into it, select items by keyboard, and confirm focus returns to the trigger.
Check the SideNav at collapsed, expanded, active, hover, nested, and mobile states.
Verify settings popovers and dialogs in jsdom and in a real browser because the native dialog and [`Popover`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Popover_API) APIs may need test shims.
Search for leftover hardcoded Tailwind colors, arbitrary hex values, and one-off hover colors after each route migration.
Run component tests, build, and at least one browser screenshot pass for each migrated route.

content.text: When using an AI coding agent, give it an explicit migration loop instead of asking for a full-app rewrite.

content.label: Paste this into your AI
content.code:
We are migrating this existing Tailwind/shadcn app to Astryx incrementally.

First run:
- astryx docs migration --dense
- astryx docs theme --dense
- astryx docs styling --dense
- astryx template AppShellTopNavWithSideNav --skeleton

Then migrate one route or shell surface at a time. Keep business logic and routing intact. Replace shadcn/Radix/Tailwind primitives with Astryx components, remove hardcoded colors, verify light and dark mode, and take screenshots before moving to the next surface.

docs.name: monorepos
docs.title: Monorepos and nested folders
docs.description: How Astryx finds the project a folder belongs to, and which version answers in a monorepo, a nested app, or a cloned repository inside another project.

content.text: Astryx searches upward from the current folder: `@astryxdesign/core` or `@astryxdesign/cli` installed there or a few folders above, else the nearest `package.json` declaring either, up to the repository root. Folders without any are outside projects.

items: A workspace member declaring Astryx is its own project, even with packages hoisted to the repository root. A root CLI answers it, as always; a member with its own Core and no CLI anywhere gets answered by the astryx command you started.
A folder without its own `package.json`, such as `src/` or `scripts/`, belongs to the project above it.
A repository that builds the CLI itself, with the CLI in `packages/cli` next to Core in `packages/core`, runs that CLI.
Folders inside another project, such as nested apps or cloned repositories, answer with the enclosing project's release.
Folder names compare as your file system compares them: a folder reached through a link, or typed in different letter case on macOS or Windows, answers like the folder itself.
In a Yarn Plug'n'Play project, Astryx cannot see the project's own CLI, so the astryx command you started answers. Run the project's CLI through Yarn (`yarn astryx`) to use it directly.

content.text: Part of {@link namespace:global}: what global mode is and how each part works.

docs.name: non-css-processing
docs.title: Non-CSS Processing
docs.description: Resolve token values outside the DOM for charts, canvas, SVG, and config objects using resolveThemeTokens() and useTheme().

content.text: Use `resolveThemeTokens()` or `resolveThemeToken()` when code outside React needs token values for a known theme and mode. Use `useTheme()` inside client components when the values should come from the nearest Theme and active mode.

content.label: Resolve tokens without React context
Resolve tokens from the nearest Theme

items: Use the returned `tokens` object as a memo dependency; it is stable until the active theme or mode changes.
Use data visualization tokens such as `--color-data-categorical-blue` for chart series instead of reusing arbitrary UI colors.
Prefer CSS variables for SVG elements when possible (`fill="var(--color-accent)"`); use token resolver APIs when an API requires a string value in JavaScript.
Use token resolver APIs for ordinary DOM styling. Use CSS variables, StyleX tokens, xstyle, or library aliases instead.

Assume the returned values reflect every CSS cascade override. They resolve tokens for the current theme and mode; local media-surface overrides and arbitrary CSS overrides may not be represented in the returned map.

docs.name: other-libraries
docs.title: Other Libraries
docs.description: Panda, Chakra, MUI, Emotion, styled-components, Theme UI, UnoCSS, and the interop checklist.

sections.title: Panda, Chakra, and Other Semantic Token Systems

content.text: Libraries like Panda CSS and Chakra UI have first-class semantic token objects. Put system CSS variables at the leaves of those objects so product code can use the library's semantic names while the system still owns the values.

content.label: Semantic token aliases
Panda-style usage
content.code:
<section
  className={css({
    bg: 'background.surface',
    color: 'text.primary',
    borderColor: 'border.default',
    p: '4',
    rounded: 'container',
  })}
/>

content.text: If a semantic-token library needs to generate its own light/dark CSS from raw values, align its mode selector with Theme (`data-theme="light|dark"`) and generate that adapter from system theme data. Otherwise it can drift from nested or runtime themes.

`MUI` expects palette slots such as primary, background, text, and divider. Map those slots to system variables for ordinary component styling. Use raw values only when MUI or your code needs to parse colors for contrast, alpha, lighten, or darken calculations.

content.label: MUI palette mapped to system vars

content.text: If MUI owns color mode in an app, generate the light and dark palette values from system theme data and keep Theme mode synchronized. If Theme owns color mode, keep both MUI schemes pointing at the same system CSS variables.

sections.title: Emotion, styled-components, Theme UI, and Styled System

content.text: Runtime CSS-in-JS libraries such as `Emotion` and `styled-components` usually accept arbitrary theme objects. Keep those objects semantic, but store system CSS variable references as the values. This keeps generated classes stable while the system updates values through the CSS cascade.

content.label: Generic CSS-in-JS theme object

content.text: Avoid rebuilding CSS-in-JS theme objects with raw color values on every mode switch. CSS variables let the class names stay the same while the browser resolves the active values.
Utility generators such as UnoCSS can put system variables in their theme config or shortcuts. Keep classes semantic (`bg-surface`, `text-primary`) and let the values point at system tokens.

content.label: UnoCSS-style config

content.text: Static utility extractors cannot see dynamically constructed class names. Prefer explicit class strings or the library's safelist/source-registration mechanism.

items: Import the reset/base CSS and a theme CSS file early enough for first paint. For production SSR, prefer built themes from `{@command theme build}` or published `/built` theme imports plus `theme.css`.
Choose one owner for color mode. Theme uses `data-theme="light|dark"` and `color-scheme` to resolve `light-dark()` tokens.
Map the external library's semantic layer to system variables by intent, not by exact naming. For example, MUI `background.paper` maps to `--color-background-surface`.
Use {@link namespace:tokens} and focused token docs when building mappings. Keep mappings small at first: text, surface/body/card/popover, border, accent, status, spacing, radius, typography, shadow.
Use token resolver APIs only for non-CSS APIs that need resolved values.

docs.name: package-and-test
docs.title: Package and test
docs.summary: Publish a package that works the first time: include everything the template needs, check the package before you publish, and try the template in a real app.

docs.name: page-template
docs.title: Page template
docs.description: Help people find a page: give it a category for `{@command search}` and template listings, and flag a sparse starting shell as a scaffold.

sections.title: Start from the generated page doc

content.text: `integration add template` writes a page doc by default. Replace its sample description, then add the page-only fields below.

content.label: templates/acme-dashboard.doc.mjs

content.text: Every field is in {@link schema:template-doc}.

items: Set `category` to the most specific supported `{Group} - {Variant}` value. Its words become search terms for `{@command search}`, and it appears in the JSON template list.
Set `scaffold: true` only for a deliberately sparse starting shell. The JSON template list reports it, so tools and galleries can tell a scaffold from a finished page.
Fields that only Astryx's own gallery reads, such as `isHiddenFromOverview`, have no effect on integration templates.

docs.name: problems
docs.title: Troubleshooting global mode
docs.description: Every line Astryx prints in global mode, what it means, and what to do. Plus the install problems package managers cause: permissions, PATH, Corepack, and Windows.

content.code: astryx: answered by CLI 0.7.2 with Core 0.7.2, outside a project

content.text: Information, not an error: it names the version that answered and why. It prints in text mode only, never with `--json`. The other forms: {@link generic:who-answers}.

sections.title: "installing CLI release … into the per-user cache"

content.code:
astryx: installing CLI release 0.6.8 into the per-user cache (once)...
astryx: waiting for another run to finish installing CLI release 0.6.8...

content.text: The project's own CLI cannot start, so Astryx is installing the CLI version equal to its Core into its cache once. The second line means another run is installing it; this one waits, up to 15 minutes. To avoid the wait, install the project's dependencies.

sections.title: "A new release of Astryx is available"

content.code:
A new release of Astryx is available: 0.7.2 → 0.7.3
To upgrade, run: npm i -g @astryxdesign/cli@latest
To upgrade, install Node >=22 (this computer runs Node 20.11.0), then run: npm i -g @astryxdesign/cli@latest

content.text: A newer version is out; run the command shown. When the newest version needs a newer Node, the second line names it first. To stop notices, set `NO_UPDATE_NOTIFIER`: {@link generic:updates}.

sections.title: "The astryx command on this computer runs CLI …"

content.code:
The astryx command on this computer runs CLI 0.6.4, which answers every folder itself.
To upgrade, run: npm i -g @astryxdesign/cli@latest

content.text: The first astryx command on your PATH is a version from before global mode, so it ignores your projects' versions. Run the command shown, or remove that install. `{@command doctor}` lists every astryx command on your PATH in its `cli-on-path` check.

sections.title: "could not get Astryx … to match this project's Core"

content.code:
astryx: could not get Astryx 0.6.8 to match this project's Core (the registry could not be reached); answering with CLI 0.7.2 instead
astryx: could not get Astryx 0.6.8 to match this project's Core (the registry does not have it); answering with CLI 0.7.2 instead
astryx: could not get Astryx 0.6.8 to match this project's Core (the release cache /home/me/.cache/astryx/releases cannot be written (EACCES)); answering with CLI 0.7.2 instead

content.text: The project's own CLI cannot start, so Astryx needs the CLI version equal to its Core, and could not get it, so the command still runs: the astryx command you started answers, as before global mode. Its answers may not match the project's Core until you fix the cause. With `--json`, `meta.answeredBy.copy` is `fallback`. Astryx waits 2 minutes before trying the download again, and 10 minutes after a second failure in a row; reinstalling the project's dependencies fixes the project's own CLI.

items: The registry could not be reached: you are offline, or a proxy blocks it. Astryx installs with npm, so set npm's `proxy`, `https-proxy`, or `registry` in your `.npmrc`, or add the CLI to the project and install its dependencies.
The registry does not have it: a private registry without the Astryx packages. Point npm's registry for `@astryxdesign` at one that has them.
The cache cannot be written: a read-only home folder, as in some containers. Point `XDG_CACHE_HOME` at a writable folder: {@link generic:ci-and-containers}.

sections.title: A global install that gets no update notice or agent guide

content.text: Astryx treats a copy as installed for your computer only when your package manager's own settings name its folder: npm's global prefix, Bun's `BUN_INSTALL`, Yarn's `global-folder`, pnpm's `PNPM_HOME`, or their defaults. A folder chosen only with a one-off flag, such as `{@pm-only yarn-classic "uses the Yarn 1 global folder" global add --global-folder ~/mine}`, is not in any setting, so Astryx treats that copy like a project's: no daily update check and no agent guide. Save the folder in your settings so Astryx knows it is a global install:

content.code:
{@pm-only yarn-classic "uses the Yarn 1 global folder" config set global-folder ~/mine}   # writes ~/.yarnrc
export BUN_INSTALL=~/mybun              # in your shell profile, for Bun

sections.title: "Core … could not be installed" outside a project

content.text: Outside a project, commands that read components (`component`, `search`, `template`, `build`, and the like) use your global version's Core. It ships beside the CLI only for some installs; otherwise your global install downloads it once into its cache in the background after a command you run online (on Windows, the first component command downloads it), and a component command before that, offline, fails with `ERR_VERSIONS_UNAVAILABLE`. Reinstalling the CLI does not help: run any command once online, and component reads work offline from then on. In CI nothing downloads in the background, so the first component command there needs the registry. The global-mode pages ({@link namespace:global}) read offline either way.

In a project with nothing installed yet, such as a fresh clone, the same commands use that Core too, and offline the error reads `This project has no Core installed, and Core <version> could not be downloaded`: install the project's dependencies (`{@pm install}`, or your package manager's), and the project's own Core answers from then on.
A run fails with `ERR_VERSIONS_UNAVAILABLE` only when nothing can answer: a command that needs Core outside a project cannot install it, or a version you requested exactly cannot be found.

content.code:
Error: No package.json found. Run this command inside an app project.
Error: No package.json found. Run this command inside an integration package.
Error: Could not find @astryxdesign/core package. Make sure you are inside the design system monorepo or have @astryxdesign/core installed.
Error: Could not find installed @astryxdesign/core (or legacy @xds/core). This folder is outside a project; upgrade migrates the code of an app project that installs @astryxdesign/core.

content.text: Commands that change an app or a package, such as `theme use`, `integration add`, `swizzle`, and `upgrade`, write nothing outside a project and say what they need. Run them in that project. Each command's doc says what it does outside a project ({@link namespace:commands}); a newer command that refuses uses `ERR_PROJECT_REQUIRED`.

items: `npm i -g` fails with `EACCES` (permission denied): do not use `sudo`. Use a Node version manager, or give npm a global folder you own: `{@pm-only npm "moves the npm global folder" config set prefix ~/.npm-global}`, then add `~/.npm-global/bin` to your PATH.

`astryx: command not found` after installing: your package manager's global bin folder is not on your PATH. `{@pm-only npm "prints the npm global folder" prefix -g}` shows npm's (its `bin` folder on macOS and Linux); `{@pm-only pnpm "sets up the pnpm global folder" setup}` adds pnpm's.

`pnpm add -g` stops with `ERR_PNPM_NO_GLOBAL_BIN_DIR`, often with Corepack: run `{@pm-only pnpm "sets up the pnpm global folder" setup}`, open a new terminal, and try again. Yarn 2 and later have no `yarn global`; use `npm i -g` instead.

Windows: npm puts `astryx.cmd` in `%APPDATA%\npm`, which must be on your PATH. If PowerShell says running scripts is disabled, run `astryx.cmd`, or allow scripts for your user with `Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope CurrentUser RemoteSigned`.
Two installs, and the wrong one runs: `{@command doctor}` outside a project lists every astryx command on your PATH, in the order your shell tries them.

content.text: This page is part of {@link namespace:global}, which explains what global mode is and how each part works.

docs.name: project-global-or-both
docs.title: Project, global, or both
docs.description: Install Astryx in each project and once for your computer: both is the recommended setup, and the two never conflict. What each side gives you, and how to set it up.

content.text: Install the CLI in each project and once for your computer. Each side does something the other cannot, and they never conflict:

items: **In the project**, the CLI version is pinned in `package.json` and the lockfile, so teammates and CI run exactly that version, with nothing fetched at run time.
**Globally**, the astryx command works in every folder, including an empty one before a project exists, and every coding agent on your computer knows Astryx through its agent guide.

**Together**, in a project the project's version always answers, even when you type the global astryx command; outside a project your global version does. Global mode never makes the project's CLI unnecessary.

rows: A pinned version in each project, plus docs, components, and search in any folder, and an agent guide for every agent
A version pinned in the repo, the same for the team and CI
No astryx command outside the project; agents elsewhere don't know Astryx
Docs, components, and search in any folder; every agent knows Astryx
Nothing pinned for a team; a project without its own CLI gets whatever version you started

content.text: In the project folder (the getting-started guide lists the other packages an app installs):

content.code:
{@pm install @astryxdesign/core @astryxdesign/cli}
{@command init}

content.text: Once for your computer:

content.code: {@pm install @astryxdesign/cli --global}

content.text: For both, do both, in either order.

sections.title: What happens when you have both

content.text: In a project, the project's version always answers, even when you type the global astryx command; outside a project, your global version does. {@link generic:who-answers}
This page is part of {@link namespace:global}, which explains what global mode is and how each part works. To start an app: {@link generic:getting-started}.

docs.name: publishing
docs.title: Publish an integration
docs.description: Publish your package to npm under the right release tag, checking it before and after.

content.text: Publish only a package that passes every check, then preview the upload with `{@pm-only npm "publishing goes through npm, which every Node install carries" publish --dry-run}`. The dry run lists the files and the tag without uploading.

content.code:
{@command doctor integration validate} && {@command doctor integration components} && {@command doctor integration templates} && {@command doctor integration docs} && {@command integration verify}
{@pm-only npm "publishing goes through npm, which every Node install carries" publish --dry-run --access public}

npm notice Publishing to https://registry.npmjs.org/ with tag latest and public access (dry-run)
+ @acme/astryx-widgets@1.0.0

content.text: Set a new `version` for each release; {@link generic:versioning} covers what counts as breaking. What each check proves is in {@link generic:checks}.
With no `files` list, npm packs every file your ignore files do not exclude, including an old `.tgz` file or an `.env` file. List what ships instead.

content.code:
{@pm-only npm "edits package.json" pkg set 'files[]=components' 'files[]=templates' 'files[]=themes' 'files[]=docs' 'files[]=codemods' 'files[]=astryx.integration.mjs'}
{@pm-only npm "builds the tarball npm publishes" pack --dry-run}

items: List only the roots you ship, and always `astryx.integration.mjs`. npm adds package.json, and a README and LICENSE when you have them.
Each later `integration add` appends its root to the list.
`integration verify` fails when a root is missing from the list, and names the root to add to `files` (the message is in {@link generic:troubleshooting}).

content.text: A scoped package is private by default, so publish it with `--access public`. Without `--tag`, npm tags the release `latest`, which is what `{@pm install @acme/astryx-widgets}` installs.
To let apps try a release first, publish it under `next`, then point `latest` at it once ready.
Install the version you published in a clean app, and run the same commands you ran against the `.tgz` file.
The full list of commands to run in an app is in {@link generic:test-in-an-app}. To help apps move to the new version, see {@link generic:upgrading}.

docs.name: quick-start
docs.title: Quick Start
docs.description: Create a new integration package or add Astryx to one you already publish.

content.text: Make the package

An integration starts as a normal npm package. Make a folder for it, create a package.json inside that folder, give the package a name, make it an ES module, then install the Astryx CLI, Core, and TypeScript for development.

items: Set `"type": "module"`: the `.js` files the CLI generates, such as a built theme, are ES modules, and Node fails to load them in a package marked `"type": "commonjs"`, which `{@pm-only npm "writes package.json" init -y}` writes on npm 11.
Start with `"exports": {}`: each component and template you add then writes the public import that `integration verify` resolves.
Run the CLI as `astryx`, which runs the `@astryxdesign/cli` you installed as a devDependency.
Component commands read Core, so they need `@astryxdesign/core` installed.

The checks compare your docs with your code through TypeScript's JavaScript compiler API, which `typescript` 5.0 through 6 has. TypeScript 7 does not ship that API: on TypeScript 7, also install `@typescript/typescript6`, its TypeScript 6 API package, and the checks use it.

content.text: Add your first integration item
An integration can ship several kinds of items. Start with a component named `AcmeCarousel`.

content.code: {@command integration add component AcmeCarousel}

component contribution added

[ok] AcmeCarousel

Declare component root ./components in astryx.integration.mjs.

- components/AcmeCarousel.doc.mjs
- components/AcmeCarousel.tsx
- package.json
- astryx.integration.mjs

content.text: `integration add` creates the component source, its `.doc.mjs`, the package export, and `astryx.integration.mjs`. Update the generated doc so the CLI understands the component, then write the component itself.
Read it back the way an app will.

content.code: {@command component AcmeCarousel}

content.text: You now have an integration package with one exported component.
Check it in every build (required)

Run `integration check --strict` in every build ({@link generic:checks}): a doc, prop, template, or link that drifts from the code then fails your build, not your users' apps. Set it up now, as the `typecheck` script, and run it.

content.code:
{@pm-only npm "edits package.json" pkg set scripts.typecheck="astryx integration check --strict"}
{@pm run typecheck}
[ok] 0 errors, 0 warnings, 0 skipped. Every check passed.

items: Run `typecheck` in CI and before every publish. When you add a `tsconfig.json`, put `tsc --noEmit && ` in front of the check so the same script checks your types.
What each check covers, and what `--strict` adds: {@link generic:checks}.

content.text: Verify and pack the package

Run `integration verify` to check that an app would see the component, then make the `.tgz` file you install next. `--pack-destination ..` writes it beside the package folder, so the next pack does not ship it.

content.code:
{@command integration verify}
{@pm-only npm "builds the publish tarball" pack --pack-destination ..}

Integration package ready

[ok] @acme/astryx-widgets@1.0.0

4 packed files; 3/3 required files present.

content.text: `integration verify` installs the packed package in a temporary app and confirms the component resolves through its public import there ({@link generic:checks}). It publishes nothing and leaves no `.tgz` file, so `{@pm-only npm "builds the publish tarball" pack}` writes `../acme-astryx-widgets-1.0.0.tgz` for the next step.
Use it in an app
Install Core, the CLI, and your `.tgz` file in a new app. The app loads your package because it is a dependency, with no config.

content.code: **Import:** `import {AcmeCarousel} from '@acme/astryx-widgets/components/AcmeCarousel';`

content.text: The next sections explain each package field and the integration file. To build the real component, continue with {@link namespace:components}.
An integration is an ordinary npm package. These six fields control how it is named, developed, checked, and published.
`peerDependencies` are packages the app supplies. `devDependencies` are packages you use while building the integration.

rows: Each add writes it into the `import` of the doc it generates. Rename before you add, or update each `import` after.
The release you publish, such as `1.0.0`
Apps see it; `astryx.integration.mjs` never repeats it.
Each component and template add writes its public import here, and `integration verify` resolves it.
Keeps private files out. When the list exists, each add appends its root and `astryx.integration.mjs`.
`@astryxdesign/core` when your code imports it; `@astryxdesign/cli`, optional, when you ship a feature that needs a newer CLI ({@link generic:versioning})
The app supplies these packages for your integration.
Lets you run the CLI, build components, and run the checks while working on the integration.

content.text: Peer ranges and releases are covered in {@link generic:versioning}; `files` and publishing in {@link generic:publishing}. Add `"typecheck": "tsc --noEmit && astryx integration check --strict"` to `scripts` so each run checks your types and that your docs, props, and links still match the code. It needs `typescript` and a `tsconfig.json`; see {@link generic:checks}.
The first `integration add` creates `astryx.integration.mjs`, and each later add updates it. You do not need to write or edit this file during the quick start.
Files in the package

items: `package.json` defines the npm package, including its name, version, dependencies, published files, and exports.
`astryx.integration.mjs` tells the CLI where the package keeps each kind of integration item.
The integration item files live under those roots. For example, a component can have `AcmeWidget.tsx` for its source and `AcmeWidget.doc.mjs` for its documentation.

content.text: Fields in the integration file

content.label: astryx.integration.mjs

content.text: The file tells the CLI where this package keeps its integration items. Edit it only when you want a custom root or another optional setting. Paths are relative to package.json, and later adds keep a custom path you already set.
Every field is in {@link schema:integration}.
Use the CLI
You can edit the package files by hand, but the CLI handles the normal workflow. These links always open the canonical command docs.

In global mode: users can also install your package for their computer, beside the global CLI (`{@pm install @astryxdesign/cli your-package --global}`). It then applies in folders outside any project, and inside a project only if the project installs it. See {@link namespace:global} and {@link generic:global-integrations}.

docs.name: reference
docs.title: Global mode reference
docs.description: Every folder global mode uses on each system, the environment variables it reads, the JSON fields it adds, its error codes, and a short glossary.

rows: Update checks and notices, and why the last notice or check did not happen (for `{@command doctor}` only)
Agent guide setting, and the links Astryx made

content.text: Every folder the agent guide is linked into: {@link generic:computer-agent-guide}.

rows: Set to anything but empty, `0`, or `false`: no update check and no notice.
Set to anything: no update check and no notice.
On Linux, move the cache and settings folders; used only when absolute.
On Windows, the cache and settings folders; used only when absolute.

content.text: Astryx reads no environment variable of its own. npm's own settings, such as its registry and proxy, apply to the versions it installs for projects.

items: `meta.answeredBy` on every successful `--json` result: `cli` (the version that answered), `core` (the Core it used, or `null`), and `copy`: `project` (the project's own CLI), `starting` (the astryx command you started, in a project with no CLI of its own), `matched` (the CLI version equal to the project's Core, when the project's own CLI cannot start), `carried` (outside a project), or `fallback` (that version could not be obtained, so the astryx command you started answered instead).

`meta.available` entries from `{@command discover}` with `source: "installed for this computer"`: an integration installed next to your global install that the project could add, with its install command in `install`.

`ERR_VERSIONS_UNAVAILABLE`: nothing can answer, such as a command that needs Core outside a project that cannot install it. When only the matching version is missing, the run answers anyway, with a warning. {@link generic:problems}

`ERR_PROJECT_REQUIRED`: a command that only works in a project ran outside one. Commands released before global mode keep the codes they already used: `theme use`, `theme remove`, and `theme add <slug>` use `ERR_THEME_INVALID`, `integration add` uses `ERR_FILE_NOT_FOUND`, `swizzle` uses `ERR_CORE_NOT_FOUND`, and `upgrade` uses `ERR_VERSION_DETECT`.
Which version answers: in a project, the project's own CLI (with only Core, the astryx command you started); outside one, your global version. {@link generic:who-answers}
Commands that change a project write nothing outside one; `doctor`, `init`, and `theme add` do something else there. {@link namespace:commands}
Integrations installed globally work only outside projects. {@link generic:computer-integrations}

The programmatic API runs in your process with the package you import and never hands off to another version; with `cwd` outside a project, its functions answer as the commands do there. {@link namespace:api}
**Global install**: the CLI installed for your computer with `npm i -g` or another package manager.
**The project's version**: the project's own CLI; it answers every command in that project. A project with only Core has none, so the astryx command you started answers.
**Cache**: the folder where Astryx keeps versions projects need but do not install.

content.text: This page is part of {@link namespace:global}, which explains what global mode is and how each part works.

docs.name: render-pages
docs.title: Pages as one HTML file
docs.description: Experimental. Render a page to one self-contained HTML file for sharing or embedding, and get the page back from it.

content.text: This command is experimental, as everything under `astryx docs cli/experimental` is: its options, its output file and its JSON may still change. Nothing else in the CLI changes because it exists.

Build the page with Astryx components as usual, then render it. The page module needs a default export; it renders on your machine with the React and Astryx packages your project installed. Outside a project (no Astryx Core or CLI installed or declared for the folder), it renders with the Astryx, React and StyleX that the CLI itself runs with, so a single page file renders anywhere, a React app included.

content.code: astryx experimental render src/app/page.tsx --out page.html

content.text: The result is ONE file with nothing beside it: the markup, only the CSS rules the page uses (from Core and from any stylesheet it imports, such as a theme), the page’s own StyleX styles, and local images as data: URIs. It runs no script and loads nothing from the network, so it opens from disk, attaches to a message, and displays inside a sandboxed frame that blocks network and script. Colors follow the viewer’s light or dark setting, and a `data-theme` of `light` or `dark` on the root element picks one. The file also carries the source of the page and of every local module, stylesheet, JSON file and image it imports, so whoever you share it with can read that code; keep secrets out of what the page imports.

What it cannot keep: anything that needs a browser while running. State, effects, click handlers and data loaded after the first paint are gone. Charts made with recharts are the exception: the render draws each chart and ResponsiveContainer a module of the page (not an installed package) imports from recharts by name (`import {LineChart} from 'recharts'`), inside the page, so a custom tick, label or shape sees the page's React context. A chart sized by its container scales to the width the page gives it, and its legend stays out of the picture: a horizontal legend takes its own row under it (above it when the legend asks for the top), and a vertical legend on one side sits beside it, on that side; in a chart of fixed size, a legend keeps the place its props give it. Charts show the data and props of the page's first render, before its effects run: when the page cannot be drawn again without a browser, or its effects change its charts or re-render the component that makes them, each chart is drawn by itself and its parts see React context defaults. A value a chart's parts read from a React context that an effect changes may still show its later value. A `chart-size` warning counts the charts the render cannot draw (one used through `import * as R`, say), and says when charts were drawn by themselves. Read browser-only values such as window inside an effect, or the render stops with ERR_RENDER_BROWSER_API.

Each warning names something that may look different from what you meant, and what to change. The most common is a component that ignores its children: `<ListItem>Save</ListItem>` renders an empty row because ListItem takes `label="Save"`. Others flag remote images (a sandboxed viewer cannot load them; save the image next to the page and import it), a `<script>`, `<link>` or `<iframe>` the page itself renders (the file promises to run and load nothing, so remove them), missing images, and output the page printed while rendering.

content.code: astryx experimental render --reverse page.html --out page.tsx

content.text: Every rendered file carries its source, so this writes the page back byte for byte; edit it and render again. A file whose source block was removed but whose markup came from Astryx components is rebuilt from that markup instead: the components, their recorded props and the text come back, while styling, icons and behavior do not, so treat it as a starting point. HTML that was never an Astryx page is refused with ERR_RENDER_NOT_ASTRYX; describe the page to `astryx build` to start one.

It writes the page, the modules, stylesheets and JSON files the page reaches through its own imports, and the images, fonts and media the render carried (however the page named them, as long as their bytes really are one): each goes where the page's relative imports find it from wherever you put the page, and a file the page imports through a path alias (`@/components/Header`) goes where your project's `tsconfig.json` or `jsconfig.json` alias points. Every file but the page goes inside the one new folder the restore creates (the topmost folder on the page's path that does not exist yet), never into a folder that already exists: a page that imports other files comes back into a new folder (`--out restored/app/page.tsx`), and a file it imports through a path alias comes back only when that alias points inside the new folder. Nor does it write a file that a test, story or benchmark runner would run by its default patterns (Jest, Vitest, Bun, AVA, Playwright, Storybook, Cypress and `node --test`: names such as `*.test.*`, `*.spec.*`, `*_test.*`, `*-test.*`, `*.bench.*`, `*.stories.*`, `*.cy.*`, and anything under `test/`, `tests/` or `__tests__/`), judged from the repository root (every folder above the file up to it), else the topmost folder with a package.json. Restored files are the sender's code: read them before you run or import them. Without `--out`, everything comes back into a new folder beside the HTML file, named after it (`page.html` comes back into `page-restored/`). A received file that carries anything else (a file the page never imports, a dotfile, `package.json`, a tool configuration, a path that leaves the folder) is refused with nothing written. A rendered file that lost its embedded source on the way (a sanitizer or an editor strips `<script>` blocks) and has no Astryx components to rebuild from is refused with `ERR_RENDER_SOURCE_DAMAGED`. An existing file is never replaced unless you pass `--overwrite`, and the refusal names every one; a generated, vendored or ignored file, and any path through a symbolic link, is not written even then. Add `--json` for the result as data: what was written, how big it is, and every warning.

docs.name: replace-a-core-component
docs.title: Replace a Core component
docs.description: Use a component replacement only when an integration must intentionally own a Core component identity.

content.text: Most components should not use `replaces`. Give a new component its own name and let apps choose it explicitly. Replace Core only when your component must become the default for one Core identity everywhere the integration is active.
Use it when

items: Your component intentionally serves the same role as one specific Core component.
Every app that loads the integration should get your component from unqualified component detail, `component --list`, search, `swizzle <Name>`, and issue routing.
You have tested both the replacement and explicit access to the original Core component.

content.text: Do not use it when

items: Your component is an alternative, variant, wrapper, or product-specific extension. Give it a unique name instead.
You only need to resolve an accidental name collision.
You want the replacement in only one screen or workflow. Replacement applies across the app wherever the integration is active.

content.label: components/AcmeSideNav.doc.mjs

content.text: Every field is in {@link schema:component-doc}.
The replacement turns on only when your package declares the first CLI release that applies it. Add this to its `package.json`:

content.label: package.json

items: Any `@astryxdesign/cli` range that starts at that release or later turns it on, including the `>=0.7.0` that `integration add doc --parent` wrote in published 0.6.4 and 0.6.5, and `integration add theme` in published 0.6.5.

Without such a range, the component keeps its own name, the Core component stays selected (a component named like its target stays ambiguous by that bare name, as before), and `doctor integration components` warns with the range to add. Apps that load such a package see no change.
`replaces` names the Core `ComponentDoc` identity, not its display label, import path, or a standalone hook.
Your component may keep a distinct name or use the same name as the target. A distinct name remains directly addressable on older CLIs that ignore `replaces`.
`--package @astryxdesign/core` always selects the original Core component, and `--package` with your package selects your component by either name.
Replacing `SideNav` replaces only that name. `SideNavItem` and the other SideNav parts stay Core components; document any parts your package provides under their own names.
`swizzle --list` lists Core components, including the one you replace. `swizzle SideNav` copies your component, and `swizzle SideNav --package @astryxdesign/core` copies the original.

Once the package declares the range, a missing target, invalid value, second replacement for one target in the same package, or a replacement named after a different Core component is an error. Without the range, `doctor integration components` reports each of these as a warning.

When several integrations replace one target, explicit configuration beats the automatic pick. Among explicitly configured integrations, the later package wins and Doctor warns. Among autolinked integrations alone, the dependency listed later in `package.json` wins and Doctor warns.

content.text: In global mode: a replacement from a package installed for the computer applies in folders outside any project; inside a project, only replacements from packages the project installs apply. See {@link namespace:global} and {@link generic:global-integrations}.

docs.name: replace-a-core-template
docs.title: Replace a Core template
docs.description: Use a template replacement only when an integration intentionally changes the default source returned for one Core template id.

content.text: Use with care: replace a Core template only when every app using this integration should receive your source for an existing Core id by default. An alternative, a product-specific variation, or a different kind of template gets its own id instead ({@link generic:start-a-template}).

items: Sharing a Core id without `replaces` does not replace Core. It makes the bare id ambiguous, so `{@command template <id>}` fails until the app adds `--package`, and `doctor integration templates` reports an accidental collision.
A replacement can keep the Core id or use its own. `replaces` is what makes it the default.

content.text: Find the exact Core id and kind first.

content.code: astryx --json template --list --package @astryxdesign/core

content.label: templates/acme-app-shell.doc.mjs

content.text: Every field is in {@link schema:template-doc}.
Declare `replaces` on the template doc, never in `astryx.integration.mjs`.
Declare the CLI floor that `integration verify` names as an optional peer ({@link generic:versioning}).

content.label: package.json

content.text: `integration verify` reports `replaces_needs_cli` when that peer is missing or too old. Without it, published 0.6.3 and earlier drop that template and hide your doc topics.
When several integrations replace the same Core template, one wins:

items: An integration explicitly listed in `astryx.config.mjs` wins over one that is only installed and picked automatically.
When several explicitly configured integrations replace the same target, the one listed later wins and Astryx reports the ambiguity.
When no integration is configured explicitly, the package listed later in the app's package.json dependencies wins. Configure the intended integration explicitly instead of relying on that order.

content.code: {@command doctor integration templates}

rows: `replaces` does not name a Core template id.
The replacement is unusable or its page/block kind differs from Core.
One package declares two replacements for a target, or several active packages contend for it.

content.text: Replacement resolution is safe by default. A missing source, invalid doc, missing target, wrong kind, or conflicting declaration never hands the Core id to a questionable replacement: Astryx reports the issue and keeps the Core template. Fix every issue before publishing.

docs.name: responsive
docs.title: Responsive
docs.description: Decide what each region does as width changes: divide, reveal, resize, or swap.

content.text: Decide what each region does as width changes. Write the responsive contract down for every region before you call the layout done.

items: Write the contract down for every region before you call the layout done
Decide per region whether it is revealed, resized, or swapped at each width
Drop a region rather than let it compete for width it does not have
Hold three regions at a width where none of them has usable space
Shrink every region uniformly instead of swapping or dropping one
Wire a breakpoint in CSS that the contract comment never mentions

content.text: Lock what each region does as width changes, and pair every line of the contract with the prop or hook that enforces it.

items: Divide: how many regions survive at each width
Reveal: which regions earn their width only when there is room, and open on demand below that
Resize: content flexes while fixed regions hold their budgets, and text stays capped by contentWidth so line length holds
Swap: navigation becomes MobileNav at the AppShell mobileNav breakpoint; the side panel becomes a Dialog or BottomSheet, driven by useMediaQuery

content.label: Contract wired to props

content.text: Verify: every contract line names a mechanism, so the comment cannot drift from the behavior.

For columns that reflow on small screens, use `Grid columns={{minWidth, max}}`. A numeric `columns` is exactly N columns at every width and never reflows: `columns={4}` on a 390px phone renders four tracks under 100px wide, and the row overflows the page as soon as their content cannot shrink to fit. `{minWidth: 240, max: 4}` renders at most four columns, each at least 240px, and drops to one full-width column when the container is narrow; `max` is what lets that last column shrink to the container, and `gap` counts toward the room the columns need.

content.label: Reflowing stat row versus a fixed week row

items: `{minWidth}` alone: as many columns as fit at the floor, no cap; a container narrower than `minWidth` overflows, so add `max` for anything that reaches a phone
`{minWidth, repeat: 'fit'}`: empty tracks collapse so present items stretch

A numeric `GridSpan` wider than the grid's current columns adds implicit columns to the whole grid; items placed before and after the span flow into them, and `columns='full'` then covers only the explicit columns. In a reflowing grid keep spans within the smallest count it can reach, or use `'full'`, which adds none

Styling that changes the room columns have to fit changes the count a reflowing shape reaches: a `columnGap` or `gap` step, inline padding on the grid, or `grid-auto-flow: column` through `xstyle`, which places items into extra implicit columns. A `className` rule replaces the computed track list only when it wins the cascade against the generated styles; prefer `xstyle` for overrides

docs.name: scaffold
docs.title: Scaffold
docs.description: Pick the shell, budget each region, and choose navigation, before any content exists.

content.text: Pick the shell, budget each region, and choose navigation, before any content exists. Shell and Navigation cover each step; these rules hold for both.

items: Decide the frame, region width budgets, and fill or capped before any content exists
State the reason for the navigation choice, or inherit the template pairing
Reserve raw px for structural widths; interior spacing uses tokens
Build content-first and wrap each section in a Card, producing a padded scroll column
Stretch prose, forms, or lists across a wide region instead of capping with contentWidth
SideNav when the nav is really filters or controls, or must hold wide elements like breadcrumbs
TopNav when top-slot ownership is unclear, or the hierarchy is deep or still growing
Both bars when the ecosystem layer is thin, so the second only wastes space
Deviate from the template navigation pairing without a stated reason

content.text: Pick the shell and budget its regions before any content exists. Structural widths are the one place raw px belongs; everything inside them uses the spacing scale.

items: Pick the frame: AppShell for nav apps, Layout with LayoutPanel in a start or end slot for multi-pane tools, or a plain content column for documents and forms
Give every fixed region a width budget, so no region has to negotiate for space at render time
Read the content to set fill or capped: tables, charts, and boards fill their region; prose, forms, and lists cap with Layout contentWidth so lines never over-stretch
Set each region container policy, rows or card grid, before writing content

content.label: A three-region tool frame

content.text: Verify: every region has a width budget, a fill-or-capped decision, and a container policy written down before any content exists.
When the frame leaves navigation open, default to SideNav: it absorbs destinations you have not planned yet. App type and destination count are guiding indicators, not determining rules.

items: SideNav, the default: grouping needed, customizable nav, items with secondary actions, or nav that collapses. Trackers, consoles, and settings usually start here

TopNav: a shallow nav you expect to stay shallow, context that must stay visible, or a control- and filter-heavy page; add a TabList for a second level. Media libraries often sit here, over grid content
Both: a genuine suite, where TopNav carries ecosystem-wide concerns (context switcher, global search) and SideNav carries product nav
Neither: messaging and feeds use a column frame of rail, nav, stream, and panel

content.label: Navigation passed to AppShell

content.text: Verify: you can state the reason in one sentence, and the choice still holds if the nav doubles in size. `{@command build "<idea>"}` names the template to start from; scaffold it and the pairing is already wired up.

docs.name: sections-and-placement
docs.title: Sections and placement
docs.description: Give your package its own docs section and place guides in it.

content.text: Give your package its own section in the docs tree with `integration add doc <name> --parent <section>`. The first run also writes the section's namespace doc.

content.label: docs/acme.doc.mjs

items: Edit its `title` and `summary`: readers see them in the docs list and at the top of your section.
The guide, `docs/deploying.doc.mjs`, gets `placement: {parent: 'namespace:acme', slot: 'guides'}`. Later runs with `--parent acme` reuse the namespace doc.
`package.json` gets the optional peer `"@astryxdesign/cli": ">=0.6.4"`, because an older CLI does not read sections; see {@link generic:versioning}.

content.text: A guide names its one home with `placement`: a namespace of your package, a slot in it, and an `order`. Its route is the section name, then the guide name.

content.code: placement: {parent: 'namespace:acme', slot: 'guides', order: 10}, // route: acme/deploying

items: Every field is in {@link schema:authored-doc-graph-fields}.
A placed guide opens only by its route, `acme/deploying`. Its bare name no longer opens it.

content.code: {@command docs acme/deploying}

content.text: A failed `placement` hides the doc: it gets no route and does not show in the docs list. `doctor integration docs` fails with `invalid_doc_graph` and names what to fix.

content.code: {@command doctor integration docs}

severity: [fail]
code:     invalid_doc_graph
message:  @acme/astryx-widgets/deploying.doc.mjs: placement.parent "namespace:cli" names no namespace; @acme/astryx-widgets declares "acme".

items: A `parent` your package does not ship, such as `namespace:cli`, "names no namespace".
A `slot` the namespace does not declare "is not a slot of namespace"; the message lists the declared slots.
The check exits 1; see {@link generic:check-your-docs}.

docs.name: see-it-in-an-app
docs.title: See it in an app
docs.description: Confirm that an app discovers the component, its package, its public import, and its documentation.

content.text: An app that installs your package sees the component beside Core components, with its package name and public import. The app needs no config.

content.code:
package: @acme/astryx-widgets

# AcmeCarousel

Cycles through slides one at a time. Use it for a small set of related cards.

**Import:** `import {AcmeCarousel} from '@acme/astryx-widgets/components/AcmeCarousel';`

content.text: `component --list` shows it as `import: @acme/astryx-widgets/components/AcmeCarousel  [@acme/astryx-widgets]`. The same commands work in your package while you build it.
Install the packed package in a test app before publishing. Then run the same detail, list, and search commands there. See {@link generic:test-in-an-app}.

In global mode: to check your package in an app, install it in that app; a copy installed for your computer is not used inside a project. To check it outside projects, install it for your computer beside the CLI. See {@link namespace:global} and {@link generic:global-integrations}.

docs.name: short-and-findable
docs.title: Short and findable
docs.description: Write short sections that people and agents find by search.

content.text: Readers open one section at a time, so give each section one idea and keep it to about 30 lines. `{@command doctor}` warns on any read over 32 KB.

items: When a section needs a second idea, split it into two sections.
Keep a topic to a few sections. When it grows past five, split it into more guides in your docs section.
A topic with more than one section reads as its section list. Readers open one section by its key, or the whole topic with `--full`.

content.text: A section's first prose block, or its first list item, is its summary in section lists and search results. Make it answer the section's question in one or two sentences.

items: The summary is cut at about 240 characters.
A code block first does not count: the summary comes from the next prose block.
Open with the answer, not with background.

content.code: build-before-you-ship  Build before you ship - Build the app, then upload the `dist` folder.

content.text: In a topic with more than one section, search ranks a section whose title matches the query, or that names it in backticks, above words in body text. Title each section with the task a reader searches for.

items: Name the task in the words a reader types, such as "Deploy to production". Avoid titles such as "Overview" or "Details".
Write field names, file names, and error codes in backticks, such as `deployTarget`: in a topic with more than one section, search treats each one as a keyword.
Other words in the summary and body match too, but rank below titles and identifiers. The summary shows under each hit, so make it answer the query.

content.text: Test a doc the way a new reader finds it: search for the question, and check that the first hit answers it. Quote a query of more than one word.

content.code: {@command search "place a doc" --type doc}

items: This query returns the section of these guides that shows how to place a doc.
Run the same search in an app that installs your package; see {@link generic:test-in-an-app}.

docs.name: side-panels
docs.title: Side panels
docs.description: Add a master-detail side panel that opens on row select instead of navigating away.

content.text: Master-detail: selecting a row opens a fixed-width side panel instead of navigating away.

items: LayoutPanel in the start or end slot of Layout, holding a fixed width budget
hasDivider to fence it from the content region; isScrollable so long detail scrolls on its own
For user-adjustable width, pair useResizable() with a ResizeHandle on the panel inner edge: after the panel in a start slot, before it in an end slot with isReversed
The handle then owns the divider, so the panel sets hasDivider={false}
Render an EmptyState when nothing is selected, so the region never collapses

content.label: Fixed panel, then the resizable form
