doc.name: Table — Sortable Columns
doc.description: Table with sortable columns, click headers to sort ascending or descending.

doc.name: Table — Striped Rows
doc.description: Table with alternating row colors and hover highlighting for easy scanning.

doc.name: useTableTreeData: Tree Table
doc.description: A file-tree table built from nested data. useTableTreeState flattens the tree into the visible rows and owns the expanded set; useTableTreeData draws the per-level indent and the expand/collapse chevron in the tree column. The two hooks are designed to work together, so this one example covers both. hasExpandAllControl adds the expand-all/collapse-all toggle to the tree column header. Collapsed branches are unmounted, not hidden.

doc.name: useTableColumnSettingsState — Column Visibility Picker
doc.description: A Table toolbar with a Columns menu of checkboxes: toggling Email updates active columns, Reset restores defaults, and the config is passed directly to useTableColumnSettings.

doc.name: useTableSortableState — Multi-Sort Orders
doc.description: Orders with no sort code of their own: useTableSortableState owns the sort state, returns the sorted orders, and hands useTableSortable a ready config. Click Customer, then Shift-click Total, to sort by customer and then by total within each customer. A line above the orders reads the current sort state from the hook.

doc.name: TabList — Fill Layout
doc.description: Tabs that stretch to fill the available width with a bottom divider.

doc.name: TabList — With Actions
doc.description: Page header pattern with tabs on the left and action buttons pushed to the right. When hasDivider is true, match the Button size to the TabList size so the tabs and actions align to a shared baseline above the divider.

doc.name: TabList — With Badge
doc.description: Tabs with notification badge counts rendered via endContent. Uses error variant for urgent counts and neutral for informational ones.

doc.name: TabList — With Icons
doc.description: Tabs with leading icons alongside text labels.

doc.name: TabList — With Overflow Menu
doc.description: Tab list with a dropdown menu for additional items that do not fit inline.

doc.name: TabList — With Status Dot
doc.description: Tabs with status dot indicators rendered via endContent to show live environment health at a glance.

doc.name: TabMenu — Basic
doc.description: An overflow menu at the end of a TabList that collects secondary tabs behind a dropdown. Use it when there are more tabs than fit comfortably inline.

doc.name: TabMenu
doc.description: TabMenu is an overflow menu within a TabList that groups additional tab options into a dropdown, showing the selected option's label as the trigger text.

doc.name: Tab
doc.description: Tab is an individual tab item within a TabList, supporting labels, icons, selected icons, and end content slots.

doc.name: Tab — Selected Icon
doc.description: A tab that changes its icon when selected.

doc.name: TextArea — Character Count
doc.description: Textareas with maxLength and a live character counter. The counter turns red when the limit is exceeded.

doc.name: TextArea
doc.description: A text area with placeholder text.

doc.name: TextArea — States
doc.description: Required, disabled, and loading textareas side by side. Shows the interactive states the component supports.

doc.name: TextArea — Validation
doc.description: All three status variants (error, warning, and success) with status messages, plus error without a message. Use to show inline validation feedback as the user types.

doc.name: TextArea — Icon
doc.description: Textareas with a leading icon that hints at the expected content, like a chat bubble for messages or a pencil for notes.

doc.name: TextInput — Icon
doc.description: Inputs with a leading icon that hints at the expected content. Use when the icon helps users identify the field faster, like a lock for passwords or an envelope for email.

doc.name: TextInput — Search
doc.description: Search input with a hidden label, start icon, and clear button. Use for toolbar and header search bars where the icon provides sufficient context.

doc.name: TextInput — Sizes
doc.description: Small, medium, and large inputs side by side. Use small in dense UIs like table filters, medium for most forms, and large for prominent single-field pages.

doc.name: TextInput — States
doc.description: Error, warning, and success validation states with status messages. Use to show users what went wrong and how to fix it.

doc.name: TextInput — Status variant
doc.description: The statusVariant prop controls whether the status message is attached to the bordered input (default, overlapping directly below) or detached from it (floating below as a separate element with spacing).

doc.name: TextInput — Types
doc.description: Text, password, and email types plus field-level features: tooltip, required, optional, description, disabled, and loading.

doc.name: Text — Colors
doc.description: All text color options (primary, secondary, disabled, placeholder, active) applied to body text to show their intended use.

doc.name: Text — Heading Levels
doc.description: All 6 heading levels (h1 through h6) rendered with Heading to show the full type scale.

doc.name: Text — Inline
doc.description: Mixing body and code text inline within a single line using the default inline display mode.

doc.name: Text — Truncation
doc.description: Single-line and multi-line text truncation with ellipsis using maxLines in a width-constrained container.

doc.name: Text — Types
doc.description: All 5 semantic text types (body, large, label, supporting, code) with their default styling from the theme.

doc.name: Text — Weight
doc.description: The 4 font weight variants (normal, medium, semibold, bold) applied to body text.

doc.name: Text — Word Break
doc.description: Compares break-word and break-all word break modes on a long unbreakable string.

doc.name: Text — Wrap
doc.description: The 4 text-wrap modes (wrap, nowrap, balance, pretty) shown in width-constrained containers.

doc.name: Theme — Apply Theme
doc.description: Wrap a subtree in Theme to apply a theme to every child component in that region.

doc.name: Theme — Nested Theme
doc.description: Nested Theme providers let a local region use a different theme without affecting the rest of the page.

doc.name: Theme — Distinct Themes
doc.description: Two visually distinct theme providers wrapping identical content to show how Theme changes the visual treatment of child components.

doc.name: Theme — Switch Themes
doc.description: Use state to switch the theme object passed to Theme and preview a different visual treatment.

doc.name: useTheme — Token Values
doc.description: Read resolved theme token values with useTheme for non-CSS consumers like SVG charts.

doc.name: Thumbnail — Disabled
doc.description: Thumbnails in the disabled state with reduced opacity. The open and remove buttons stay focusable and announced as disabled, and call nothing.

doc.name: Thumbnail — Gallery
doc.description: A row of clickable thumbnails with labels that open a detail view. Use for image attachment lists where users need to preview and manage uploads.

doc.name: Thumbnail — Removable
doc.description: Thumbnails with a remove button overlay. The close button uses APCA luminance detection to stay visible on both dark and light images.

doc.name: Thumbnail
doc.description: A thumbnail with an image and label.

doc.name: Thumbnail — States
doc.description: All visual states side by side: image loaded, placeholder, skeleton loading, and upload overlay. Demonstrates the full lifecycle of a thumbnail from empty to loaded.

doc.name: TimeInput — Constrained
doc.description: Time inputs with min/max constraints limiting selection to specific windows. Use to prevent out-of-bounds selections for appointments, reservations, or shift scheduling.

doc.name: TimeInput — Formats
doc.description: 12-hour, 24-hour, and seconds formats side by side. Use 12h for US-centric UIs, 24h for international or technical contexts, and seconds for precise timing.

doc.name: TimeInput — Increment
doc.description: Time input with a custom step increment. Arrow keys jump by the specified interval (e.g. 15 minutes) for quick slot-based scheduling.

doc.name: TimeInput
doc.description: A time input that uses the browser/OS picker on touch by default and Astryx typed entry on fine pointers.

doc.name: TimeInput — States
doc.description: Default, disabled, error, warning, and success states. Use status messages to give users clear feedback about their time selection.

doc.name: Timer — Formats
doc.description: Elapsed compact units and stopwatch clock notation shown from the same start time.

doc.name: Timer — Inline
doc.description: A Timer composed into status copy while inheriting the surrounding typography.

doc.name: Timer — Typography
doc.description: Timer using its Timestamp-matched default typography and an emphasized override.

doc.name: Timestamp — Auto
doc.description: Auto format that shows relative time for recent dates and switches to the full date for older ones. The default choice for most use cases.

doc.name: Timestamp — Colors
doc.description: Timestamp rendered in each available color variant: primary, secondary, disabled, and active.

doc.name: Timestamp — Formats
doc.description: All display formats side by side: date, date_time, time, and their system equivalents. Use date and date_time for user-facing UI, system variants for logs and dev tools.

doc.name: Timestamp — Relative
doc.description: Relative time labels from seconds to months ago, with hover tooltips showing the full date. Use in feeds, comment threads, and activity logs.

doc.name: Timestamp — Timezone
doc.description: Timestamps with the timezone abbreviation appended. Enable isTimezoneShown for audiences across time zones, like audit logs or team calendars.

doc.name: Timestamp — Tooltip time zones
doc.description: Hover tooltips that show one instant across several time zones or formats. Use tooltipEntries when readers must compare zones, like an incident log carrying both the reader's time and the event's origin zone.

doc.name: Toast — Action
doc.description: Persistent toasts with a trailing button or link so the user can act on the notification, like undoing a delete or viewing a report.

doc.name: Toast — Deduplication
doc.description: Prevent duplicate toasts with uniqueID. Use ignore to keep the first toast, or overwrite to replace it with updated content like a progress percentage.

doc.name: Toast — Dismiss
doc.description: Show a persistent toast and dismiss it programmatically using the function returned by useToast. Use for long-running operations that need manual cleanup.

doc.name: Toast
doc.description: Imperative toast notifications triggered with useToast and rendered in the toast viewport.

doc.name: Toast — Stacking
doc.description: Multiple toasts stacking vertically with smooth enter and exit animations. Click repeatedly to see how toasts queue and dismiss.

doc.name: Toast — Types
doc.description: Info and error toast variants side by side. Info toasts auto-dismiss after 5 seconds, error toasts persist until the user dismisses them.

doc.name: useToast — Settings Saved
doc.description: Shows a toast from the function useToast returns: a "Settings saved" confirmation with an Undo action, a uniqueID so pressing the button again replaces the toast instead of stacking another, and an error toast when the request fails.

doc.name: ToggleButtonGroup
doc.description: ToggleButtonGroup manages a set of ToggleButtons with single-select or multi-select behavior for options like view modes or filters.

doc.name: ToggleButtonGroup — Vertical
doc.description: A vertically stacked ToggleButtonGroup using the vertical orientation, shown with both single-select and multi-select behavior, ideal for sidebar-style option lists and vertical toolbars.

doc.name: ToggleButton — Color
doc.description: Toggle buttons with colored icons in the pressed state. Shows accent-colored toolbar formatting and semantic reaction colors (yellow star, red heart, blue bookmark).

doc.name: ToggleButton — Group
doc.description: Toggle button groups in single-select and multi-select modes. Single selection acts as a view mode switcher; multiple selection forms a formatting toolbar.

doc.name: ToggleButton — Icon Swap
doc.description: Icon-only toggle buttons that swap between outline and solid icons when pressed. Use for actions like favorite, bookmark, or mute where the icon itself communicates the state.

doc.name: ToggleButton — Label
doc.description: Toggle buttons with visible text labels that show a font weight shift on press. Use when the icon alone is not enough to communicate the action.

doc.name: ToggleButton — States
doc.description: Default, pressed, disabled, and loading states of a standalone toggle button. Shows how visual treatment changes across states.

doc.name: Tokenizer — Clear
doc.description: Tokenizer with a built-in clear-all button for bulk removal of all selected tokens. On touch screens, clear through the sheet's Clear all.

doc.name: Tokenizer — Creatable
doc.description: Free-text tokenizer for creating custom tags and a combined create-or-search pattern. Use when users need to enter values that may not exist in a predefined list.

doc.name: Tokenizer — End Content
doc.description: Tokenizer with an action button in the end slot. Use for inline actions like applying selections alongside the input.

doc.name: Tokenizer — Icon
doc.description: Tokenizer with a leading search icon to visually reinforce the search behavior.

doc.name: Tokenizer — Max Entries
doc.description: Tokenizer with a maximum selection limit. The input hides automatically when the limit is reached, preventing further additions.

doc.name: Tokenizer — Overflow
doc.description: Tokenizer with overflow truncation when unfocused. Inline mode pushes content down on expand; layer mode overlays without shifting layout. Overflow modes apply to the inline field.

doc.name: Tokenizer
doc.description: A tokenizer with preset tags and search source.

doc.name: Tokenizer — States
doc.description: Tokenizer in disabled, error, warning, and success states. Use to communicate validation feedback or lock a selection from editing.

doc.name: Token — Clickable
doc.description: Interactive tokens that respond to clicks. Use for toggleable filters or tokens that open a detail view when selected.

doc.name: Token — Colors
doc.description: All 11 color variants in default and disabled states. Use color to categorize entities or convey status at a glance.

doc.name: Token — End Content
doc.description: Tokens with trailing content like a count badge or status indicator after the label. Use for notification counts, item quantities, or compact status info.

doc.name: Token — Icon
doc.description: Tokens with a leading icon that identifies the entity type. Use when the icon helps users recognize the token category faster, like a user icon for people or a tag icon for labels.

doc.name: Token — Removable
doc.description: Tokens with a dismiss button for selections the user can undo. Use in multi-select fields, active filters, or any list of user-chosen items.

doc.name: Toolbar — Bulk Actions
doc.description: A compact toolbar with the muted variant for showing bulk selection actions. Use when the user selects multiple items in a list or table and needs quick access to batch operations.

doc.name: Toolbar — Card Header
doc.description: A toolbar as a card header with a left-aligned title and icon actions on the right. Use Toolbar instead of LayoutHeader when your card header has interactive actions; Toolbar adds start/end slot layout, keyboard navigation, and automatic size cascading. If the header is just a title with no actions, a LayoutHeader or Section is enough.

doc.name: Toolbar — Sizes
doc.description: Small, medium, and large toolbars side by side. The size prop cascades to child buttons and inputs automatically. Use small in dense UIs like cards, medium for most cases, and large for spacious layouts.

doc.name: Toolbar — Table Filter
doc.description: Filter bar above a table: a search box leads the row, each field beside it is a closed trigger that doubles as its own filter chip — the bare field name unset, the whole clause once set — and the clauses fold from the end into a count as the row narrows, followed by a live result count, a clear all, and a column picker. Use to search, filter, and narrow flat rows of records such as jobs, orders, tickets, or users.

doc.name: Toolbar — Three Slot
doc.description: A toolbar with start, center, and end content using the three-column grid layout. Use when you need a centered title or heading with navigation and actions on either side.

doc.name: Toolbar — Tab Navigation
doc.description: A toolbar with tabs in the start slot and an action button at the end. Use as a card or section header when content is split into tabs with a primary action alongside.

doc.name: Tooltip — Action Bar
doc.description: Tooltips on an action button bar with contextual descriptions.

doc.name: Tooltip — Hook Usage
doc.description: Tooltip using the useTooltip hook for programmatic control.

doc.name: Tooltip — Inline Text
doc.description: Tooltips on inline text terms for definitions.

doc.name: TopNavHeading — Basic
doc.description: A product heading with a logo inside a TopNav, linked to the home page. Use as the leading brand element of a top navigation bar.

doc.name: TopNavHeading
doc.description: Demonstrates TopNavHeading with a logo and text, both as a plain display and as a clickable link.

doc.name: TopNavItem — Basic
doc.description: Navigation links inside a TopNav with one item marked as selected. Use for top-level pages of an application.

doc.name: TopNavItem
doc.description: Demonstrates TopNavItem with selected, icon, disabled, and default states.

doc.name: TopNavMegaMenuFeaturedCard — Basic
doc.description: A promotional card with a title, description, and call-to-action link. Pass it to the featured slot of a TopNavMegaMenu to highlight announcements.

doc.name: TopNavMegaMenuFeaturedCard
doc.displayName: Top Nav Mega Menu Featured Card
doc.description: Demonstrates TopNavMegaMenuFeaturedCard with a title, description, and CTA link inside a mega menu.

doc.name: TopNavMegaMenuItem — Basic
doc.description: Rich link items with an icon, title, and description. Use inside the items slot of a TopNavMegaMenu to describe each destination.

doc.name: TopNavMegaMenuItem
doc.description: Demonstrates TopNavMegaMenuItem with icons, titles, and descriptions inside a mega menu.

doc.name: TopNavMegaMenu — Basic
doc.description: A mega menu trigger inside a TopNav that opens a panel of rich link items. Use when a navigation section has multiple destinations worth describing.

doc.name: TopNavMegaMenu
doc.description: Demonstrates TopNavMegaMenu with items and a featured card in the mega menu panel.

doc.name: TopNavMenu — Basic
doc.description: A dropdown menu inside a TopNav built from an items array with icons and descriptions. Use to group related destinations under a single trigger.

doc.name: TopNavMenu
doc.description: Demonstrates TopNavMenu with a hover-triggered dropdown containing items with icons and descriptions.

doc.name: TopNav — Centered Navigation
doc.description: Navigation layout with center-aligned nav items flanked by a logo heading and end actions.

doc.name: TopNav — Enterprise Dashboard
doc.description: Full-featured navigation bar with icon-labeled nav items, search, notifications, and a primary CTA.

doc.name: TopNav — Hover Menu
doc.description: Navigation bar with a hover-triggered dropdown menu showing product items with icons and descriptions.

doc.name: TopNav — Mega Menu
doc.description: Marketing-style navigation with a full-width mega menu featuring product items and a promotional featured card.

doc.name: TopNav — Multiple Dropdowns
doc.description: Navigation bar with multiple hover-triggered dropdown menus that auto-close when switching between them.

doc.name: TopNav — With Logo
doc.description: Navigation bar with a branded logo icon, heading link, nav items, and a profile action.

doc.name: TreeList — File Tree With Icons
doc.description: File browser tree with folder and document icons distinguishing directories from files.

doc.name: TreeList — Interactive Settings
doc.description: Settings tree with clickable items and a documentation link.

doc.name: TreeList — Mailbox Tree
doc.description: Email folder tree with unread badge counts.

doc.name: TreeList — Navigation Tree
doc.description: Navigation tree with a selected item for the current page.

doc.name: Tree List — Variants
doc.description: The `variant` prop controls whether hierarchy guide lines are shown: `lineGuides` (default) draws connector lines between parent and child rows, while `noGuides` relies on indentation alone. It is orthogonal to `density`, which controls spacing.

doc.name: TypeaheadItem — Basic
doc.description: A typeahead whose results are rendered with TypeaheadItem, adding a secondary description below each label. Use inside renderItem to keep custom results visually consistent.

doc.name: TypeaheadItem
doc.description: Typeahead with custom item rendering using TypeaheadItem for avatars and descriptions.

doc.name: Typeahead — Limited Results
doc.description: Typeahead with a capped dropdown showing at most three results.

doc.name: Typeahead — Search Field
doc.description: Search input with icon and suggestions on focus.

doc.name: Typeahead — With Helper Text
doc.description: Typeahead with a description below the label.

doc.name: Typeahead — With Validation
doc.description: Typeahead with an error validation message.

doc.name: useAnimator — Playing cards
doc.description: A playing card that follows a drag: a gentle release springs it back on its release velocity, and a quick flick throws it away with momentum before the next card is dealt. A Discard button moves it off from the keyboard, fading it in place under Reduce Motion, and the discard is announced. Built only on the public useAnimator hook.

doc.name: useDragToSnapPoints — Playing card on three places
doc.displayName: useDragToSnapPoints — Playing card on three places
doc.description: A playing card that a sideways drag moves between three places: a slow release settles on the nearest, a quick flick carries to the next, and a release moving back returns where it started. Buttons settle it from the keyboard, and the new place is announced. Built only on the public useDragToSnapPoints hook.

doc.name: usePanGesture — A draggable box
doc.description: The smallest pan example, in two forms side by side: the usePanGesture hook and the createPanGesture factory. The factory takes any element, React or not. Each card names its API, follows a drag from a finger, a mouse or a pen, and springs back, with the same StyleX styles. A starting point for a draggable tile, a swipe or any drag-and-release gesture.

doc.name: usePanGesture — A playing card (advanced)
doc.description: An advanced usePanGesture example: a playing card follows a drag, settles back on a gentle release and flies off on a quick flick, while a Discard button deals the next card from the keyboard and announces it. Drag, settle and throw are StyleX styles driven by React state. A pattern for swipe-to-dismiss, card decks and flick gestures.

doc.name: VisuallyHidden — Live Region
doc.description: A polite aria-live region announces visual-only state changes to assistive technology.

doc.name: VisuallyHidden — Structural Heading
doc.description: Give a visually implicit section an accessible name so screen-reader users can navigate to it.

doc.name: VisuallyHidden — Supplementary Context
doc.description: Stat cards whose trend arrows get screen-reader-only text, so a change like +12% is read as an increase from last month. Use to make terse visual data accessible.

doc.name: VStack — Basic
doc.description: A heading and paragraphs stacked vertically with a consistent gap. Use VStack whenever siblings should flow top to bottom with even spacing.

doc.name: VStack
doc.description: Demonstrates VStack arranging items vertically with different gaps.

doc.name: AI Chat Landing
doc.description: Zero-state entry surface centered on a single composer with suggestion chips instead of history, sized for the moment before any content exists. The empty counterpart to a transcript.

doc.name: AI Chat Conversation
doc.description: Transcript of alternating turns carrying mixed rich content inline (markdown, code blocks, collapsible tool-call output) beside a resizable artifact panel that holds generated output while the stream keeps scrolling.

doc.name: Blank
doc.description: Bare scaffold: one heading slot, one empty content region, no navigation and no chrome. The starting point when every other layout imposes more structure than wanted.

doc.name: Canvas Editor
doc.description: Layered artboard workspace: document tabs over a layer rail, a fixed-size frame you zoom on a muted backdrop, and an inspector of position, type, and filter fields that retargets to the selected layer. Objects hold a coordinate rather than reflowing, so moving one never moves another.

doc.name: Centered Hero
doc.description: Symmetrical centered stack (headline, short blurb, paired call-to-action buttons) resting on one wide full-bleed picture, with nothing on either flank competing.

doc.name: Checkout Wizard
doc.description: Multi-step checkout, cart, order, and payment wizard with a running summary that recalculates as answers change. It adapts to its host width, renders the summary first on narrow surfaces, validates every forward path, and completes locally without sending payment.

doc.name: Classic Gallery
doc.description: Uniform grid of equal-ratio media tiles under a centered intro, with filter tabs that narrow the set in place. Regular rhythm, unlike the variable-height masonry variant.

doc.name: Contact Form
doc.description: Flat single-column form mixing control types (text, pill toggles, dropdowns, long free-text) landing on one full-width submit. No steps, no branching, no summary rail.

doc.name: Course Detail
doc.description: Long-form sales page for a single offering, in two columns — read the pitch, then enroll from a sticky rail. The main column holds a preview poster with a fact row, an about block with skill chips, a module syllabus whose sections collapse module by module, an instructor card, reviews with a scored-aspects panel, and a FAQ; the rail holds the price, a self-paced or cohort start picker, and a weekly-pace slider that computes a finish date. The shape for any offering with a curriculum and a purchase panel — a course, class, masterclass, bootcamp, workshop, or training.

doc.name: Service Monitoring Dashboard
doc.description: Always-on analytics with a triage rail: status-colored tiles with sparklines, multi-series time charts over a switchable window, and an independently scrolling alert column that folds into the content when narrow.

doc.name: Funnel & Cohort Dashboard
doc.description: Analytics for sequence and retention questions, pairing two shapes a plain dashboard cannot hold: a staged funnel where each step reads as drop-off against the one before, and a two-axis cohort matrix rendered as a heatmap.

doc.name: Data Dashboard
doc.description: Comparison-heavy analytics behind a persistent filter bar: tiles that each carry an inline sparkline and several period-over-period deltas, then segmented breakdowns underneath. Every number is shown against another number.

doc.name: Portfolio Dashboard
doc.description: Analytics for a value-over-time question: balance and change tiles above a stacked area chart of composition through time, closing on a ranked table of the largest contributors.

doc.name: Project Status Dashboard
doc.description: Status analytics mixing progress and time-axis shapes: a completion donut, a horizontal timeline of dated bars against a today marker, a per-owner table with progress and status, an at-risk list, and a burndown.

doc.name: Executive Summary Dashboard
doc.description: Report-shaped analytics with a prose rail beside the charts: a scorecard of headline numbers with period deltas and status coloring, goal-attainment bars, a trend grid, and a written commentary column that folds beneath the content when narrow.

doc.name: Analytics Dashboard
doc.description: Three-band analytics: a row of headline tiles, then charts, then supporting tables, all re-reading from one global filter bar. Breadth over depth, a summary surface rather than a drill-down.

doc.name: Order Detail
doc.description: Single-record detail in two columns: a summary header with status and actions, a repeating line-item list, a totals block that sums it, and a chronological activity timeline in the rail. The shape for any record holding children plus a history: a customer order with shipping, an invoice, a transaction, or a job.

doc.name: Documentation Design
doc.description: Reference article alternating prose with live rendered examples: an interactive preview, a property table, paired do and don't comparisons, and copyable code blocks.

doc.name: Documentation Technical
doc.description: Reference article ordered as sequential numbered steps with code at each stage, plus callout cards for prerequisites and onward links. A linear walkthrough rather than a browsable reference.

doc.name: Documentation Catalog
doc.description: Reference landing that is pure wayfinding: a banner above a grid of category cards linking into sections, with no article content on the surface itself.

doc.name: Page Editor
doc.description: Three-pane authoring workspace: a source palette on one flank, a live canvas in the middle, and an inspector that retargets to whatever is selected. Drag and drop to reorder, edit to see it render immediately.

doc.name: File Explorer
doc.description: Hierarchical browser that drills through nested levels as adjacent columns rather than replacing the list each time, with breadcrumb history, switchable list and grid density, and a metadata pane for the selected node.

doc.name: Two-column Form
doc.description: Form split into two columns beneath a hero header: inputs on one flank, a persistent context panel opposite that stays put while the fields scroll. Flat, single submit, no steps.

doc.name: Dialog Wizard
doc.description: Step through a short flow in a dialog, overlay, or popup launched from the page underneath, which stays where it was. Compact step markers and a pinned action row inside a constrained width, rather than the full page a wizard usually gets. Best for two to four short steps — setup, invite, schedule, onboarding — where losing the context underneath would cost more than the flow is worth.

doc.name: Inline Wizard
doc.description: Accordion wizard stacking every step in one column: the active step expands in place while finished ones collapse to a single line carrying their result and a way back in. Steps that run themselves expand into a nested stepper that ticks check by check and halts the column where one fails. Best when later steps depend on what earlier ones decided.

doc.name: Form Wizard
doc.description: Linear multi-step form that moves through one panel at a time, with a horizontal progress track pinned above rather than running down a rail, so every step keeps the full content width for its fields. Only the current step renders, unlike an accordion where each section expands into one long scrolling form. Each advance is validated, and a step left broken stays flagged to jump back to.

doc.name: Vertical Wizard
doc.description: Multi-step wizard with the steps in a fixed left rail that stays visible while the form scrolls, plus a side panel whose guidance follows the focused field. Suits long or unequal steps carrying uploads, previews, and dense review metadata. As width tightens the guidance drops first, then the rail rotates into a horizontal stepper above the form.

doc.name: Gallery Hero
doc.description: Centered stack (headline, short blurb, call-to-action buttons) resolving into a multi-image photo grid rather than one wide full-bleed picture, so the imagery reads as a set.

doc.name: IDE
doc.description: Dense multi-pane workspace of resizable, collapsible regions: a hierarchy tree on one flank, tabbed documents in the middle, a docked drawer along the bottom, an inspector opposite. Drag a divider to resize or collapse any of them.

doc.name: Incident Console
doc.description: Dense row queue with an inspector: severity-coded rows grouped by status, a saved-search filter bar, a segmented status control, and a resizable detail pane for the selected row. Rows, not cards, sized for scanning volume.

doc.name: Kanban Board
doc.description: Horizontal lanes of draggable cards where the column itself is the status, so drag and drop between lanes is the state change. Fixed columns, variable-height cards.

doc.name: Card Grid
doc.description: Searchable, browsable card grid with filter tabs and a real empty state: uniform tiles organized by topic, narrowing in place, with no detail surface behind them.

doc.name: Login Card
doc.description: Credential form inside an elevated centered card, third-party provider buttons separated from the fields by a divider, secondary sign-up and legal links beneath.

doc.name: Login Split
doc.description: Credential form filling one half of a two-pane split, full-bleed media holding the other. Same fields as the card variant, but the layout carries brand imagery.

doc.name: Login SSO

docs.name: AlertDialog

usage.description:
AlertDialog asks the user to confirm a destructive or irreversible action before it happens. Use it for things like deleting content, revoking access, or discarding unsaved changes.

It implements the WAI-ARIA APG [Alert Dialog pattern](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/alertdialog/): `role="alertdialog"`, a title linked by `aria-labelledby`, a consequence description linked by `aria-describedby`, focus moved into the dialog on open and returned to the trigger on close, and no dismissal by clicking outside. Escape cancels.

AlertDialog passes its requested width through to Dialog, which clamps the surface to the container and dynamic viewport with token gutters. Generic Dialog footers should wrap, but Dialog does not own action semantics or order; consumer composition controls that. AlertDialog owns its confirmation semantics: above 640px, actions render horizontally and may move onto another row; at 640px and below, the destructive action appears above Cancel and both buttons fill the footer width. Button labels retain their standard single-line behavior. The breakpoint follows available width, not pointer or hover capability. The body scrolls when block space is constrained.

The two actions are tracked as one group under every pointer, the way iOS tracks the actions of an alert: the action under the pointer highlights as soon as it is pressed, the highlight follows the pointer from one action to the other, and the release runs the action under it. Releasing off both actions runs nothing. The keyboard and assistive technology keep the click of each button.

For cases where you want to show an alert without managing open state, use the `useImperativeAlertDialog` hook: call `alert.show(options)` and render `alert.element` in your tree.

bestPractices.description: Make the action button label specific: "Delete project" is better than "OK" or "Confirm".
Describe what will happen in the description so the user knows the consequences before confirming.
Keep the cancel button as the least-destructive focus target. On narrow screens the destructive action is visually and structurally above Cancel, but Cancel still receives initial focus.
Use concise, specific action labels. Above 640px, complete buttons may move onto another row; at 640px and below, the destructive action appears above Cancel and both buttons fill the footer width.
Use AlertDialog for non-destructive actions; use a standard Dialog instead.
Rely on color alone to signal danger; the action label itself should say what will happen.
Close the dialog from onAction before the work finishes; hold it open with isActionLoading and call onOpenChange(false) when the action settles.

params.name: element
params.description: The element to animate. The animator writes its `translate`, `scale`, `rotate` and `opacity`, and while it moves an inline `will-change` for them, merged with any it already has and restored 500 ms after its last motion; nothing else, so lay it out and style it as usual. Use one animator per element: two on one element overwrite each other.

returns.name: animate
returns.type: (target: {x?, y?, scale?, rotate?, opacity?}, options?: {velocity?}) => Promise<void>
returns.description: Springs the given channels to `target` from wherever they are on screen, on the state-change motion Astryx's components use, and resolves when they arrive (or as soon as a later call takes them over). `x` and `y` are px, `scale` is 1 at the element's size, `rotate` is degrees and `opacity` runs from 0 to 1. Pass `velocity` (units per second, such as a drag's release velocity) to start with it; without it a channel keeps the velocity it has on screen, so interrupting a motion never jumps.

returns.name: decay
returns.description: Coasts the given channels from a release velocity in their units per second, slowing as a scroll view's momentum does, and resolves when they stop (or as soon as a later call takes any of them over); opacity stops at 0 or 1. The distance follows from the velocity: use it to fling something away, then remove or reset it.

returns.name: set
returns.description: Puts the given channels at these values at once, ending their motion: follow a finger with it, frame by frame.

returns.name: get
returns.description: Every channel's value on screen now.

returns.name: getVelocity
returns.description: Every channel's velocity on screen now, in units per second.

returns.name: stop
returns.description: Halts every channel where it is on screen.

returns.name: destroy
returns.description: Stops every motion and lets the element go; the element keeps the values it shows. Call it when you remove the element or no longer animate it.

usage.description: Animates one element with the motion Astryx's own components use, without React. `animate` springs an element to new values on the state-change motion, `decay` flings it with the momentum of a released scroll view, and `set` moves it directly, so a card can follow a finger, snap back and be thrown away. Use the `useAnimator` hook in React. To animate an area's layout as its items change, use `useAnimatedLayout`; for what a component already animates, such as a sheet's detents or a carousel's snapping, use the component's own props.

bestPractices.description: Start every `animate` that follows a drag with the release velocity, so the element carries on as it was thrown.
Reach every state an animation shows without the animation too: a key, a button or a menu item that calls the same code.
`await` the promise before removing an element you animate out, and call `destroy` once it is gone.
Read the element’s position from layout while it moves: `get` gives the value on screen, wherever the motion runs.

accessibility.name: Keyboard and assistive technology
accessibility.description: An animator moves an element; it adds no way to act. Give every action an animation stands for a control a keyboard and a screen reader can reach, such as a button that discards a card, and have it call `animate`, which Reduce Motion turns into a fade in place. Keep `decay` for a throw the person made: Reduce Motion keeps the momentum of a coast, as it continues that throw. Keep focus on an element that stays on screen: move it before you fling its element away.

accessibility.name: Reduce Motion
accessibility.description: When the person asks for reduced motion, every call is planned for them. On a touch screen a move or a scale becomes a short opacity cross-fade: the element fades out where it was and fades back in where it lands. With a mouse it lands at once. A decay of `x` and `y` keeps its momentum, as it continues the throw the person made; a decay of `scale`, `rotate` or `opacity` is planned like a move. No option turns this off.

docsDense.description: Animates one element (x, y, scale, rotate, opacity) with Astryx's motion, without React.

paramDescriptions.element: The element to animate; one animator per element.

returnDescriptions.animate: (target, {velocity?}) => Promise<void>; springs on the state-change motion.
returnDescriptions.decay: ({x?, y?, scale?, rotate?, opacity?}) => Promise<void>; coasts from a release velocity.

usage.description: Spring with animate, fling with decay, follow a finger with set. Reduce Motion: a cross-fade on touch, at once with a mouse; decay keeps its momentum.

bestPractices.description: Pass the release velocity to animate after a drag.
Read layout for the position mid-motion; use get.

usage.description: AppShell is the page shell for an application. It provides slots for top navigation, side navigation, banners, and main content. Use it as the root wrapper for every page. It handles responsive mobile navigation and skip-to-content automatically. Configure side nav collapse on SideNav with its collapsible prop.

bestPractices.description: Choose the right height: use "fill" for dashboards with internal scrolling and "auto" for pages that grow with content.
Set `contentPadding` based on content type: 4 for forms and settings, 0 for tables and dashboards.
Give every nav slot an accessible name. AppShell renders TopNav and SideNav as separate navigation landmarks, and a screen reader lists them by name, so pass `label` to each one.
Start the page heading inside `children`. AppShell owns the skip link, the banner landmark and the main landmark, but it renders no heading, so the first heading in the content area is the page h1.

On phones, opt the page into the full screen with `viewport-fit=cover` in the viewport meta tag (`width=device-width, initial-scale=1, viewport-fit=cover`). AppShell then extends its header under the status bar and out to the screen sides, and keeps the header's items and the end of the content inside the device's safe area. An installed web app can also draw under the status bar with `<meta name="apple-mobile-web-app-status-bar-style" content="black-translucent">`. In landscape only the header is inset: an inline SideNav and the content's sides still reach under a notch, so keep content padding there. A shell with no header region or phone top bar keeps no top inset; keep top padding there.
Nest one AppShell inside another; it's the outermost layout frame.
Use for sub-page layouts; use Layout for content areas within AppShell.
Add your own skip link or <main> element. AppShell already renders both, and a second main landmark makes the first ambiguous.

usage.description: Maintains a fixed width-to-height ratio for its children as its container resizes. Use it for media containers like videos, images, thumbnails, or any content that needs consistent proportions. It takes its width from the container and derives its height from the ratio, so it needs an ancestor with a definite width.

bestPractices.description: Express the ratio as a fraction for readability — `ratio={16 / 9}` rather than `ratio={1.78}`. It is a number, so the string form `ratio="16/9"` is a type error.
Use for media that needs consistent proportions across screen sizes.
Use `fit="cover"` for images and video so the component sizes the child; the child should not repeat `width`/`height`/`objectFit` styles.
Pass one child. With `fit` set, every direct child is stretched to fill the box, so put an overlay or caption inside a single wrapper child rather than passing it as a second child.
Describe media children with `alt`, or `alt=""` when the image is decorative. AspectRatio adds no role and no accessible name of its own, so the child carries the whole accessible description.

For a breakpoint-dependent ratio, override the ratio responsively: pass an `aspectRatio` rule via `xstyle` (StyleX), or override `aspect-ratio` from your own unlayered CSS under a `@media`/`@container` rule; component styles live in the `astryx-base` cascade layer, so unlayered consumer CSS wins. Give an `xstyle` rule a `default` branch alongside the conditional one (`{default: 3, '@container ...': '3 / 2'}`); with only the conditional branch the ratio is unset outside the query and the box collapses.
Use for general layout containers; use standard layout components instead.
Nest AspectRatio containers; one level is sufficient.
Constrain the height on its own. The width comes from the container, so a `height` or `maxHeight` by itself clamps the box off ratio; pair it with `width: "auto"` to size from the height instead.
Place it in a shrink-to-fit parent such as `inline-flex`, `width: fit-content` or a floated box. It contributes no intrinsic width there and collapses to zero.

anatomy.name: Ratio box
anatomy.description: The outer element that holds the aspect ratio and clips overflow. Carries the `astryx-aspect-ratio` theme target, and the elliptical clip when `shape` is `ellipse`.

anatomy.name: Content slot
anatomy.description: A wrapper that fills the ratio box and positions the child. With `fit` set it also sizes the child; without it the child styles itself.

props.name: ratio
props.description: Aspect ratio as width/height (e.g. 16/9, 1). Emitted as a class-level declaration (never inline), so `xstyle` rules or unlayered consumer CSS can override it responsively.

props.name: shape
props.description: Container shape. Both respect the `ratio`. `ellipse` clips to an oval (a circle when `ratio={1}`).

props.name: fit
props.description: How the child is sized inside the ratio box. `cover` fills and crops media, `contain` fills and letterboxes, `center` keeps the natural size centered. When omitted, the child styles itself.

props.name: children
props.description: Content positioned absolutely to fill the container.

props.name: xstyle
props.description: StyleX styles for layout customization (margins, positioning, sizing). Must be a stylex.create() value, not an inline style object like style={{}}.

docsDense.description: maintains specific aspect ratio for children

docs.name: Avatar

usage.description: Avatar represents a person or team with a profile photo, initials, or a default icon. Use it in comment headers, contact lists, chat messages, user cards, and anywhere you need to identify someone visually.

bestPractices.description: Always pass a name so the avatar can show initials if the photo fails to load, and so screen readers can announce who it represents.
Pick a size that matches the context: xsm or sm for inline mentions, md or lg for lists and cards, xl for profile headers.
Add a status dot when knowing someone's availability matters, like in chat or team views.
When wrapping an Avatar in your own Tooltip or HoverCard, set tooltip={false} so the built-in name tooltip does not overlap yours.
Give every interactive avatar (href or onClick) a name or alt. It is the control's accessible name, and it warns in development when it is missing.
Rely on a status label to name an interactive avatar. "Online" says nothing about where the link goes.
Use Avatar for logos, product images, or anything that isn't a person or team. Use an image or icon instead.
Use xstyle or className to override shape. Use the shape prop instead so themes can control it globally.

anatomy.name: Photo
anatomy.description: The profile image, loaded from the src URL. Shown when available.

anatomy.name: Initials
anatomy.description: The first letter, digit or emoji of the first and last words of the name; punctuation is skipped. Shown when no photo is available. A name with no letters, digits or emoji shows the default icon instead.

anatomy.name: Default icon
anatomy.description: A generic person silhouette. Shown when there is no photo or name.

anatomy.name: Status dot
anatomy.description: A small indicator in the bottom-right corner showing availability (online, away, busy). Each variant pairs colour with a distinct shape so status does not rely on colour alone.

vars.name: --_avatar-group-overlap
vars.description: Negative inline offset applied to every avatar stacked in an AvatarGroup; the group pads its start edge by the same amount so the first avatar stays inside it. Set from the group size; a more negative value tightens the stack.
vars.default: set at runtime from the group avatar size (px)

vars.name: --_avatar-radius
vars.description: Border radius of the avatar wrapper, content, focus ring, and the AvatarGroupOverflow "+N" chip. Set per shape variant by shapeStyles.

docs.description: Displays a user avatar with image, initials fallback, and optional status indicator.

props.name: src
props.description: Primary image source URL.

props.name: fallbackSrc
props.description: Fallback image when primary fails.

props.name: name
props.description: User name for initials and alt text.

props.name: alt
props.description: Alt text (falls back to name).

props.name: size
props.description: Avatar size: named sizes are 'xsm' (20px), 'sm' (24px), 'md' (36px), 'lg' (48px), and 'xl' (128px); numeric sizes must be one of the pixel values listed in the type. Inside an AvatarGroup, the group's size always overrides this prop, including when the group uses its default size.

props.name: shape
props.description: Shape variant of the avatar. 'circle' (default) stays fully round. 'rounded' uses the element radius token so it matches UI corner rounding and can be set globally via theme. 'square' has no radius. Status dot positioning adapts automatically: 4-o'clock on circle, bottom-right corner on rounded/square.

props.name: status
props.description: Corner content for status indicators. AvatarStatusDot reports its `label` to the avatar, which composes it into the accessible name (e.g. "Jane Doe, Online") so screen readers announce the status. Reporting goes through context, so it still works when the dot sits inside a wrapper component of your own.

props.name: tooltip
props.description: Tooltip shown on hover and keyboard focus. Omitted or true shows the avatar's name; a string shows that text instead; false shows no tooltip. Not auto-disabled when wrapped in your own Tooltip/HoverCard. Set tooltip={false} if you supply your own overlay. No tooltip is shown when tooltip is true/omitted and there is no name.

props.name: href
props.description: When set, the avatar renders as an interactive link (`<a>` or a custom link component) pointing here. This follows the same element-swap rule as Button. Requires a meaningful accessible name via `alt` or `name`: an interactive avatar without one warns in development. Inside an AvatarGroup, interactive avatars share a single Tab stop and are reached with arrow keys.

props.name: as
props.description: Custom link component used when `href` is set (e.g. `next/link`). Overrides the provider-level LinkProvider default. Only applies with `href`.

props.name: target
props.description: Link target attribute. Only applies with `href`.

props.name: rel
props.description: Link rel attribute. Only applies with `href`.

props.name: onClick
props.description: Click handler. When set without `href`, the avatar renders as a focusable `<button type="button">`. Requires a meaningful accessible name via `alt` or `name`: an interactive avatar without one warns in development.

usage.description: Avatar displays a user or entity's profile picture with automatic fallback to initials or a default icon. Use it alongside user information to visually represent people, teams, or entities throughout the interface.

bestPractices.description: Always provide a name prop so the component can generate meaningful initials and alt text when the image fails to load.
Use the status slot with AvatarStatusDot to indicate online presence or availability when relevant to the context.
Give every interactive avatar (href or onClick) a name or alt. It is the control's accessible name, and it warns in development when it is missing.
Use Avatar for decorative images or logos that aren't representing a person or entity. Use an image or icon component instead.

docs.name: AvatarStatusDot
docs.description: Size-aware status indicator dot that reads avatar size from context and scales proportionally. Each variant pairs a colour with a distinct built-in shape (filled, ring, minus) so status is never conveyed by colour alone (WCAG 1.4.1).

props.name: variant
props.description: Semantic variant pairing colour with a distinct shape: success = filled green dot, neutral = grey ring, error = red dot with a minus bar.

props.name: label
props.description: Accessible label describing the status. Inside an Avatar it is composed into the avatar's accessible name (e.g. "Jane Doe, Online"); the Avatar root is role="img", which prunes child semantics, so the composed name is how the status reaches assistive tech. Standalone dots expose role="img" with this label directly.

props.name: icon
props.description: Icon centered inside the dot (hidden at tiny sizes). A rendered icon replaces the built-in shape glyph, so use a different icon per status.

docsZh.name: AvatarStatusDot

props.name: variant
props.description: 语义变体，颜色与形状配对：success = 绿色实心点，neutral = 灰色圆环，error = 带横杠的红色点。

props.name: label
props.description: 描述状态的无障碍标签。在 Avatar 内会被合成进头像自身的无障碍名称（如 "Jane Doe, Online"）——Avatar 根元素为 role="img"，会裁剪子元素语义，因此合成名称是辅助技术获知状态的途径。独立使用时状态点直接以 role="img" 暴露该标签。

props.description: 居中显示在状态点内的图标（tiny 尺寸时隐藏）。渲染的图标会替换内置形状标记，请为每个状态使用不同的图标。

docs.name: AvatarGroup

usage.description: AvatarGroup displays multiple avatars in an overlapping row with an optional overflow indicator. Uses a compositional API: pass Avatar children directly so each avatar can carry its own props (status dots, click handlers, etc.).

bestPractices.description: Slice the list yourself and pass only the avatars you want visible; 3-5 is typical. The group renders exactly the children it is given and never slices for you.
Use AvatarGroupOverflow for custom overflow content like a popover trigger or "add member" button.
Pass status dots, click handlers, or tooltips directly on each Avatar child.
Wrap an Avatar child in HoverCard or Tooltip to show more on hover; the avatars still overlap. Set tooltip={false} on the wrapped Avatar so its built-in name tooltip does not compete.

Make avatars interactive with href or onClick to link to profiles. Interactive avatars share a single Tab stop; arrow keys move between them, and the group announces a keyboard hint to assistive tech. This follows the WAI-ARIA APG roving tabindex technique for managing focus in a composite: https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/practices/keyboard-interface/#kbd_roving_tabindex
Don't nest AvatarGroups; use a single group with all avatars.
Don't set size on the child avatars. The group's size wins over each child's own size prop, including when the group leaves size at its default, so a child's size is silently ignored inside a group.

anatomy.description: Avatar elements that form the overlapping row. Each can have its own props.

anatomy.name: Overflow indicator
anatomy.description: A "+N" circle at the end showing hidden count, or a custom AvatarGroupOverflow slot.

The group's size always overrides each child Avatar's size, including when the group uses its default size.

props.description: Ref forwarded to the root element.

props.name: xstyle

usage.description: AvatarGroup 以重叠排列方式显示多个头像，并可选择显示溢出指示器。使用组合式 API：直接传入 Avatar 子元素，每个头像可携带自己的属性。

bestPractices.description: 自行切分列表，只传入需要显示的头像，通常 3-5 个为佳。组件只渲染传入的子元素，不会自动切分。
使用 AvatarGroupOverflow 自定义溢出内容，如弹出触发器或"添加成员"按钮。
直接在每个 Avatar 子元素上传递状态点、点击处理器或工具提示。
可以用 HoverCard 或 Tooltip 包裹 Avatar 子元素以在悬停时显示更多信息，头像仍会重叠。请在被包裹的 Avatar 上设置 tooltip={false}，避免与内置的名称提示冲突。
不要嵌套 AvatarGroup，使用单个组包含所有头像。
不要在子头像上设置 size。分组的 size 会覆盖每个子 Avatar 自身的 size，即使分组使用默认值也是如此。

docs.name: AvatarGroupOverflow
docs.description: Overflow indicator for AvatarGroup. Shows a compact count for hidden avatars and can render custom count text or act as a button.

props.name: count
props.description: The number of hidden avatars. Used for the default `+N` label and the accessible label.

props.name: children
props.description: Optional custom count text rendered inside the indicator. Omit to use the default `+N` label.

props.name: onClick
props.description: Callback fired when the overflow indicator is clicked. When provided, the indicator renders as a focusable button.

props.name: ref
props.description: Ref forwarded to the overflow indicator element.

props.name: xstyle
props.description: stylex.create() value — not an inline style object.

usage.description: AvatarGroupOverflow appears at the end of an AvatarGroup to summarize people who are not shown individually. Use it when a group is sliced to a small number of visible avatars but the hidden count still matters.

bestPractices.description: Pass the real hidden count to `count` so the accessible label matches the visible indicator.
Use short custom text such as `+12` or `99+`. The indicator is circular for short counts and grows into a pill for wider counts so the number always fits.
Provide `onClick` when the overflow opens a member list, popover, or detail view.
Do not pass custom text that disagrees with `count`; `count` continues to provide the accessible label.
Do not use long labels inside the indicator; place longer participant details next to the group instead.

anatomy.name: Count label
anatomy.description: The compact `+N` or custom count text displayed inside the circular indicator.

usage.description: Badge highlights a status or category at a glance. Use it sparingly: only when a value represents a distinct state (Active, Failed) or a grouping tag (Engineering, Design). Most metadata (dates, durations, counts, descriptions) should be plain description text, not badges.

bestPractices.description: Every status badge steals attention. Only badge states where the user needs to notice or act: errors, warnings, items requiring follow-up. If no action is needed, plain text is fine.
Use success, warning, and error variants only for system status that demands attention: "Failed", "Degraded", "Action Required". These have bold solid backgrounds designed to stand out.
Use color variants (blue, purple, teal, etc.) for category tags that group or classify items: team names, content types, priority levels.
Keep labels to one or two words. If you need more detail, put it in surrounding text instead of the badge.
Add an icon when it helps identify the badge type quickly, but always include a text label alongside it.

Apply a "success" badge to every healthy/active/normal item. If all rows show green "Active" badges, none stand out; the badge adds noise, not information. Show only the states that need user attention (errors, warnings, pending actions).
Use badges for metadata. Durations ("6h window"), counts ("12 trigger types"), dates, and descriptions are not statuses or categories; use description text (Text with type="supporting") instead.
Use semantic status variants (success, warning, error, info) for categories or informational content. These are visually loud and should only indicate system state.

Repeat the same badge in every row of a table or list. If the same value appears in most rows, it's not adding information; use plain text for common states and reserve badges for the exceptional ones.
Make badges clickable; they are read-only indicators. Use a button or link if the user needs to take action.

usage.description: Banner shows a persistent message at the top of a page or section. Use it for form errors, system updates, maintenance notices, or success confirmations that the user needs to see until they act on it.

bestPractices.description: Pick a status that matches the message: info for updates, warning for caution, error for problems, success for confirmations.
Use the card container inside page content and the section container for full-width messages that span the entire page.
Make info and success banners dismissable. Keep error banners visible until the user fixes the issue.
Keep titles short and scannable: "Payment failed" not "There was a problem processing your most recent payment."
Use Banner for short-lived messages that disappear on their own; use Toast instead.
Stack multiple banners with the same status; combine related messages into one banner.

Set collapsible={false} when the user needs the content to act on the message, like the list of fields that failed validation. Keep the default toggle when the detail is long enough to bury the banner's own message.

Banner status controls color and icon only; it does not create a live region. Announce async outcomes from the transition handler with useAnnounce. Pass role="alert" only for an urgent message the person must act on now: Banner puts it on the title and description, so controls, endContent and supporting content are not read as part of the alert. Do not also announce that message with useAnnounce.
Rely on the status color or icon alone to carry meaning; say which status it is in the title text, because the icon is decorative to a screen reader.

docs.name: BottomSheet

children.children: Adjust the properties below, then open the preview.

docs.description: A mobile touch sheet that rises from the bottom edge, with animated entrance and exit, a grab handle, optional drag-to-resize snap points, and purpose-controlled dismissal. Like Dialog, it is a padded container: content starts at the theme's bottom-sheet padding (--spacing-4 by default), and a lone Section child or bleed children such as Table and Divider align against it. At the top the content always starts below the grab bar's 24px band, which is not padding a child escapes, so the first row never sits under the bar; scrolled content passes beneath it. A sheet always owns a native <dialog>; inside the deprecated BottomSheetSwitcher the switcher presents and closes that dialog as the flow moves between steps. In both modes, ref and shared DOM props target the visual panel <div>. Sheets stack: a sheet opened while another is open sits on top of it, the covered sheet stays mounted and recedes, and one scrim covers the page. A sheet that closes as another opens in the same update is replaced by it, with the step-to-step handoff a multi-step flow needs.

props.name: isOpen
props.description: Whether a standalone sheet is open. Fully controlled; pair with onOpenChange. Omitted only inside the deprecated BottomSheetSwitcher, which drives its steps itself.

props.name: onOpenChange
props.description: For a standalone sheet, called when it requests an open-state change. Automatic calls follow purpose: info dismisses on Escape, scrim click, or swipe; form dismisses on Escape only; required never dismisses implicitly. Omitted only inside the deprecated BottomSheetSwitcher, which drives its steps itself.

props.name: finalFocusRef
props.description: Optional explicit focus-return target for a standalone sheet. Use when the opener can remount or the active element is not a reliable trigger, such as an adaptive presentation switch. Always focused when the sheet closes on its own or last; when a modal sheet is still open beneath, focus returns into that sheet (to this element if it is inside it, else the revealed panel). Omitted only inside the deprecated BottomSheetSwitcher, which drives its steps itself.

props.name: purpose
props.description: Controls implicit dismissal behavior, matching Dialog. info allows Escape, scrim click, and swipe-to-dismiss. form protects entered data by blocking scrim click and swipe while allowing Escape. required blocks every implicit dismissal path and uses role='alertdialog'. Explicit controls may still update the controlled state. Works for standalone and BottomSheetSwitcher-managed sheets.

props.name: sheetId
props.description: Deprecated with BottomSheetSwitcher: give each step its own standalone sheet with isOpen instead. Still works as released: the unique ID of this sheet inside a BottomSheetSwitcher, which opens it when activeSheet matches; omit isOpen and onOpenChange when sheetId is used.

props.name: label
props.description: Accessible label for the sheet. Required; the sheet has no built-in heading to derive a name from.

props.name: children
props.description: Sheet content in a scrollable area. The named body is keyboard reachable while overflowing. Forward Tab entry may move directly to the first native link or button; input controls, composite widgets, and nested scroll areas retain the body stop. Shift+Tab from a delegated first child skips the body. Fitting content adds no body stop. The internal observed content box preserves block flow and percentage heights. If it includes a text-entry control that can bring up the mobile keyboard, use height='tall' and keep the sheet fully expanded while editing.

props.name: padding
props.description: Internal padding of the sheet content using the spacing scale, matching Dialog. When omitted, uses the theme default for bottom sheets (--spacing-4 unless the theme sets padding on bottom-sheet). A lone Section child escapes the padding, and bleed children such as Table and Divider compensate against it. Use 0 for edge-to-edge content that supplies its own inset. Whatever the padding, the block-start inset is never less than the grab bar's height (--spacing-6), so resting content starts below the bar.

props.name: height
props.description: How tall the sheet is. Named budgets: 'hug' fits its content up to 92% of the viewport, 'capped' is a scrolling mid-height panel (~62%), and 'tall' is a pinned near-full panel (~92%) for content that streams in. Or pass a number (px) / CSS length for a custom budget. Give snapPoints to let the user drag between heights. On shorter viewports the sheet fills the available height. Only a fully expanded 'tall' sheet provides mobile-keyboard accommodation: it stays put and scrolls each focused control above the keyboard. Hug, Capped, numeric and CSS-length heights never do, and a Tall sheet stops doing it the moment the user drags it to a shorter detent, resuming when they drag it back. Outside that state the sheet neither moves nor adds keyboard scroll space, and the browser's own focus reveal is left in place; on iOS that reveal can shift the whole page. This accommodation applies where the visual viewport shrinks for the keyboard, as in Safari on iOS, Firefox for Android and Chrome on Android, where the sheet places the focused control just above the keyboard as it comes up, and the control rides the rest of Gboard’s slide up, and the slide down after it loses focus; a hide Chrome reports late, such as Back, rides down from Chrome’s report (`astryx docs browser-support`).

props.name: snapPoints
props.description: Extra heights the sheet can rest at when dragged; its own height is always the tallest stop, and omitting this gives a sheet that only opens and closes. Each stop is the sheet's visible height: a number is a viewport fraction (0.5 is half the screen), '50%' the same in CSS, '320px' an absolute length. A stop of a quarter of the sheet or less is a peek: it slides away instead of reflowing, and thins the scrim.

props.name: hasScrim
props.description: For a standalone BottomSheet, whether to render a scrim, the semi-transparent overlay that covers and blocks the background. true (default) uses showModal(): top layer, native focus containment, ::backdrop scrim, body scroll lock, and tap-scrim-to-dismiss when purpose='info', with the background inert. A scrim sheet also takes part in stacking (see Stacking below). false presents the sheet in the top layer as a manual popover (below the Popover API support floor, show() in page stacking order as a reduced fallback) with no scrim, no focus trap and no scroll lock, leaving the page behind interactive and scrollable; a no-scrim sheet neither stacks nor is stacked on, but no-scrim steps replace each other with the same handoff. A no-scrim sheet shown while a modal (a scrim sheet or a Dialog) that does not contain it is open is inert under that modal and stays beneath it (show(), no page-level z-index) until that modal has gone, then enters the top layer; a modal mid-exit counts as gone, and rendered inside the modal the sheet enters the top layer at once. In a multi-step flow, set hasScrim the same on every step.

usage.description:
A mobile touch surface for filters, actions, forms, and detail views that should rise from the bottom of the viewport. For a multi-step flow, give each step its own sheet and one state value that names the open step (see Replacing a sheet); open a second sheet over the first when a step should stay visible beneath it.

Stacking. Every sheet keeps its own isOpen. Open a sheet while another scrim sheet is open and it stacks on top: the sheet beneath stays mounted with its scroll position and inputs, recedes behind the new one (the nearest covered sheet shrinks to 0.96 and lifts 8px, deeper ones to 0.92 and 16px), and is blocked from pointer, keyboard, and assistive technology by the top sheet's modal dialog. The sheets can be siblings, live in separate components, sit inside another sheet's content, or sit inside a BottomSheetSwitcher step; a whole switcher is one level, and switching its step in place does not change its position. Nothing moves in the DOM: each sheet's dialog stays where it is written, and no wrapper component is needed.

Order is open order. The top sheet is the one presented most recently that is still open; a sheet that closes and reopens comes back on top. When several sheets open in one update (a deep link into a flow), there is no open order between them, so tree order decides: a sheet below the sheets rendered in its content, siblings in the order they are written. That order is right in the first painted frame.

One scrim. Only the bottom sheet's backdrop dims the page; the backdrops of the sheets above it are transparent, so a stack never darkens per level. The dim holds steady while sheets push and pop, and if the bottom sheet closes while sheets remain above it, the next sheet's backdrop takes over in the same frame.

Dismissal. Escape, a tap on the scrim, a downward swipe, and a platform close request (Android back, a close watcher) reach only the top sheet, through that sheet's own onOpenChange, and that sheet's purpose applies: required blocks all of them, form blocks the scrim and the swipe. Nothing closes a whole stack at once; set every sheet closed in one update when a flow is done and they leave together.

Closing a covered sheet from code. Sheets rendered inside the closing sheet's content are part of it: they are presented only while it is open and leave with it. Their isOpen stays yours, as with a Dialog rendered in a closed Dialog: nothing is written to it, and a nested sheet that is still open when its host reopens is presented again, on top. Set it closed yourself when the flow is done. Sheets above the closing sheet that are not in its content stay open and keep their order; the closing sheet slides out from beneath them, and if it owned the scrim, the sheet above takes it over.

Replacing a sheet. Close the top sheet and open another in the same update (one state value that names the open step does this) and the new sheet replaces it instead of stacking on it: the new sheet rises above the one it replaces; if the replaced sheet is taller it moves down to meet the new sheet's top edge at the same time; the replaced sheet fades only after both motions finish, and is inert and hidden from assistive technology from the start. The scrim holds steady throughout, with no dip; focus moves into the new sheet; and when the flow closes, focus returns to the element that opened its first sheet, whichever sheet closed last. This is the handoff the deprecated BottomSheetSwitcher ran between its steps; a multi-step flow needs no switcher: give each step its own BottomSheet and one state value. A replace happens only when exactly one sheet closes and one opens in the update, the closing sheet was the top sheet of its stack, and the move was made from inside it (the control last pressed, or with no recent press the focused element, was in the closing sheet, as a step's own Continue or Back button is); a covered sheet closing while a sheet opens, a close and an open in different updates, or a close and an open driven from a control outside the closing sheet (two unrelated owners acting at once) keep the ordinary push and pop motion and their own focus return. A replace over an open stack runs one level up and leaves the sheets beneath covered. Non-modal sheets (hasScrim={false}) replace each other the same way, with no scrim: they are hosted in the browser top layer as manual popovers, so the entering step orders above the retained one with no page-level z-index, and toasts raised before or while the sheet is open stay above it. Below the Popover API support floor (Tier 2 in the browser support guide) the sheet falls back to show() in page stacking order: usable, but with no promise over later page content. A non-modal sheet returns focus to its opener on close only while focus is still inside it; focus taken elsewhere on the live page stays there.

Focus. Opening a sheet, modal or not, focuses its data-autofocus field (a TextInput with hasAutoFocus) in every browser. Without one, focus goes wherever the engine's native dialog focusing steps land: the panel in Chromium, the first focusable control in Firefox. A step entering as a replacement also focuses a data-autofocus descendant first, so a flow that opens on a field keeps the keyboard on it. Closing the top sheet returns focus into the sheet it reveals: to the control that opened it when that control is still there, otherwise to the revealed sheet's panel. When the last sheet closes, the standalone rules apply: finalFocusRef, else the element that opened the sheet, with a focus ring only after keyboard input. When every sheet of a stack closes in one update, focus returns once, to the bottom sheet's finalFocusRef or opener, after the last dialog has closed.

Caveats. A Dialog, AlertDialog, or Popover opened from a sheet paints above the sheet and does not make it recede; a sheet opened from inside that Dialog paints above the Dialog and stacks over the sheet beneath. Sheets with hasScrim={false} stay out of the stack entirely (they replace each other, but never stack, recede, or take the scrim). A sheet React hides (a suspended Suspense boundary, Activity mode="hidden") leaves the stack and closes its dialog; when it is shown again it is presented again, on top. Only sheets rendered in the same document stack; a sheet inside an iframe is its own stack.

bestPractices.description: Use for mobile-first surfaces (filters, share sheets, quick actions) where the content should rise from the bottom edge.

For a drill-in, open the next sheet over the current one and keep each sheet's isOpen where its data lives; a detail sheet can sit inside the list sheet that opens it, right next to the row. Close every sheet in one update to close the whole flow.
Pick the starting height that fits the content: 'hug' for short bounded content, 'capped' for lists, and 'tall' for forms or streaming/resizing content.
Use purpose='form' to protect entered data from scrim clicks and swipes while keeping Escape available; reserve purpose='required' for flows that must end through an explicit action.
Don't make the sheet content overly long. Break it into steps, each its own sheet, with one state value naming the open step; moving on replaces one with the next.

Don't stack more than two or three sheets: deeper sheets share the second recede step and the user has to pop them one at a time. Replace steps instead (close one, open the next in one update) when they do not need to stay visible.
